articles.title: Nigeria, World Bank partner to tackle AfCFTA digital trade barriers - ITWeb Africa
articles.summary: Nigeria, World Bank partner to tackle AfCFTA digital trade barriers  ITWeb Africa
articles.full_text:
Nigeria is working with the World Bank Group to identify regulatory gaps affecting digital trade as the country seeks to align its domestic policies with the African Continental Free Trade Area’s Digital Trade Protocol.
According to the Nigerian AfCFTA Coordination Office, the initiative will examine how the country’s pending digital economy legislation and planned e-commerce policy can be aligned with continental rules intended to facilitate cross-border digital commerce.
Patience Okala, the office’s national coordinator and chief executive, said the regulatory gap analysis aims to ensure that the protocol, its annexes and Nigeria’s domestic laws and policies operate consistently.
The development comes as African governments seek to reduce regulatory obstacles that prevent businesses from expanding their digital services beyond national borders.
Nigeria has identified Ghana, Egypt, Rwanda, South Africa and Kenya as priority markets for domestic businesses seeking regional expansion. Regulators from the five countries had visited Lagos to examine market-access requirements and identify areas where regulatory processes could be aligned or mutually recognised, Okala said.
Differences in national regulations can complicate cross-border e-commerce, digital payments, electronic transactions and the handling of data.
Businesses operating across multiple African markets may need to navigate different requirements for digital documentation, consumer protection, payment services and regulatory compliance. For smaller companies, these differences can increase the cost of entering new markets and make it harder to scale services across the continent.
In an August 2026 report, the World Bank argued that Africa’s next phase of economic integration depends on reducing trade and regulatory friction and improving connections between national systems. The report identified digital networks, payment infrastructure, customs procedures and services as important components of a more integrated regional market.
The AfCFTA Digital Trade Protocol provides a continental framework for addressing some of these challenges. Its implementation, however, depends on countries translating regional commitments into domestic laws, regulations and operational systems.
Nigeria’s proposed National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill is part of that process. The legislation is intended to establish a broader legal framework for the country’s digital economy, while the planned e-commerce policy is expected to support the development of online commercial activity.
The regulatory review will help identify where existing rules and proposed measures need to be aligned with the continental framework.
In related news, Nigeria has also been selected as one of three pilot countries for the Africa Digital Access and Public Infrastructure for Trade initiative, alongside Egypt and Kenya.
The programme, run by the AfCFTA Secretariat and the Tony Blair Institute, aims to advance interoperability between digital systems and support implementation of the Digital Trade Protocol.
A team has been inaugurated in Nigeria to work on the initiative, according to Okala.

articles.title: Africa’s 20 Largest Economies in 2026: South Africa Leads, Kenya Rises, Tanzania Slips - Uchumi360
articles.summary: Africa’s 20 Largest Economies in 2026: South Africa Leads, Kenya Rises, Tanzania Slips  Uchumi360
articles.full_text:
Ready
South Africa remains Africa’s largest economy at about US$489 billion in 2026, but the continent’s economic hierarchy is shifting rapidly as Kenya, Ghana, Ethiopia, DRC and Côte d’Ivoire gain scale. Tanzania ranks 12th while Uganda continues to close the gap.
Africa’s economic hierarchy is changing faster than the familiar rankings of the past would suggest. South Africa remains the continent’s largest economy in nominal terms at an estimated US$489.08 billion in 2026, followed by Egypt at US$442.89 billion and Nigeria at US$386.67 billion. But beyond the top three, a more consequential reshuffling is taking place. Kenya has consolidated its position as East Africa’s largest economy at US$151.15 billion, Ghana has climbed to eighth, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo have both crossed US$120 billion, Côte d’Ivoire has moved above Tanzania, and Uganda is now approaching the US$75 billion threshold.
The ranking, based on the IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook framework and the country figures supplied for 2026, captures more than economic size. It reflects the combined effect of real growth, inflation, exchange rates, commodity cycles, demographic expansion and revisions to national accounts. The IMF’s October WEO confirms that the database covers GDP, inflation, trade and other macroeconomic indicators, with projections extending several years ahead.
That distinction matters because nominal GDP measured in US dollars can move sharply even when the underlying economy changes more gradually. A country can grow strongly in real terms but slip in the ranking if its currency depreciates heavily against the dollar. Another can move rapidly upward because of higher commodity revenues, currency appreciation or rebasing. The ranking therefore provides a useful picture of economic scale, but not a complete measure of living standards, productivity or development.
South Africa Holds The Top Position, But Its Growth Remains Weak
South Africa’s estimated US$489.08 billion economy keeps it comfortably at the top of the African ranking, ahead of Egypt and Nigeria. Yet the size of the economy contrasts with weak real expansion. The IMF expects South Africa to grow by only about 1 percent in 2026, making it one of the slowest growing economies among Africa’s top 20.
That creates a familiar South African paradox. The country retains the continent’s deepest financial markets, largest industrial base, sophisticated corporate sector and major mining industry, but growth remains constrained by infrastructure weaknesses, power supply challenges, logistics bottlenecks, unemployment and low investment.
South Africa remains number one because of the scale accumulated over decades. The more important question is how long it can preserve that position if its growth remains close to 1 percent while several economies further down the ranking expand at 5 percent, 6 percent or more.
Egypt, at US$442.89 billion, is much closer. The IMF projects Egypt’s real GDP growth at about 5.1 percent in 2026, meaning the gap between Africa’s first and second largest economies can narrow significantly if Egypt sustains stronger expansion and stabilises its currency.
Nigeria Is Still Enormous, But No Longer Africa’s Unchallenged Giant
Nigeria’s position at US$386.67 billion marks a striking reversal from the years when it regularly appeared as Africa’s largest economy.
The country remains the continent’s most populous market and one of its largest oil producers, but currency depreciation has dramatically changed its nominal GDP position in US dollars. The naira’s weakening has reduced the dollar value of domestic output, even when measured economic activity has continued growing in local terms.
The IMF projects Nigeria’s real GDP growth at about 4.2 percent in 2026. That is stronger than South Africa’s, but still below the pace being recorded by several emerging African economies.
Nigeria therefore demonstrates one of the central weaknesses of nominal GDP rankings. Economic size in dollars depends partly on what happens in foreign exchange markets. A country can remain economically significant, add millions of consumers and increase production while falling down the ranking because its currency loses value.
The result is that Africa’s largest population no longer automatically produces Africa’s largest nominal economy.
North Africa Still Controls A Large Share Of The Top Five
North Africa remains heavily represented near the top. Egypt ranks second, Algeria fourth at US$331.89 billion and Morocco fifth at US$195.63 billion.
Algeria’s position remains closely connected to hydrocarbons, with oil and gas revenues continuing to support export earnings, government finances and the broader economy. The IMF expects growth of about 3.8 percent in 2026.
Morocco’s US$195.63 billion economy is almost US$40 billion larger than Angola’s and more than twice Tanzania’s. Unlike several commodity dominated economies, Morocco has gradually built a wider production base across automotive manufacturing, aerospace components, tourism, phosphates, agriculture, logistics and increasingly renewable energy and industrial exports. The IMF projects Moroccan growth at roughly 4.5 percent in 2026.
The broader lesson is that nominal scale is increasingly being determined not only by resource endowment, but by whether countries can build diversified sectors capable of generating exports, domestic value addition and stable foreign exchange earnings.
Angola Has Rebuilt Its Position Through Oil, But Diversification Remains The Test
Angola ranks sixth at US$157.30 billion, ahead of Kenya. Its economic position remains heavily linked to oil, which continues to dominate export earnings and public revenue. The IMF expects Angola to grow around 4.4 percent in 2026. That growth gives Angola room to consolidate its position, but the structure of the economy remains a vulnerability. Oil can push GDP upward quickly when prices and production are favourable, but it also exposes the country to sharp external shocks when global markets turn.
Angola’s ranking therefore says more about economic scale than diversification. The long term challenge remains converting hydrocarbon wealth into manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, services and industries capable of sustaining growth after oil’s relative importance declines.
Kenya Has Become East Africa’s Clear Economic Leader
Kenya’s rise to seventh place at US$151.15 billion is one of the most significant shifts in Africa’s economic ranking.
The country now stands more than US$55 billion ahead of Tanzania and almost US$79 billion above Uganda. Kenya has built its scale through a relatively diversified economic base that includes financial services, telecommunications, transport, agriculture, tourism, real estate, professional services, manufacturing and a large regional corporate sector. Its growth is not the fastest in East Africa. The IMF expects Kenya to expand by about 4.5 percent in 2026, compared with 9.2 percent for Ethiopia, 6 percent for Tanzania and 6.2 percent for Uganda.
Kenya’s advantage is the stock of economic activity already accumulated. Nairobi has become a regional headquarters for banks, technology companies, professional firms, development institutions and multinational corporations. Its financial system is deeper than most regional peers, while the country has also built strong export sectors in horticulture, tea, tourism and business services.
The ranking also shows why East Africa is becoming a larger part of Africa’s overall economic story. Kenya, Ethiopia, DRC, Tanzania and Uganda all feature within the continent’s top 13 economies.
Ghana’s US$128.64 Billion Economy Is One Of The Ranking’s Biggest Stories
Ghana’s rise to eighth place at US$128.64 billion places it ahead of Ethiopia, DRC, Côte d’Ivoire and Tanzania. That is significant because Ghana has only a fraction of the population of Ethiopia or Tanzania. Its ranking reflects the recovery of the economy, currency movements, commodity exports and the size of its services and extractive sectors. The IMF projects Ghana to grow about 5.7 percent in 2026.
Ghana’s position also illustrates how quickly African rankings can change after periods of currency and debt instability. A stronger cedi, lower inflation, fiscal adjustment and recovery in domestic activity can substantially increase the dollar value of the economy even before structural changes are fully visible. For this reason, Ghana’s eighth place should be watched over several years before being interpreted as a permanent new equilibrium.
Ethiopia Is Growing Faster Than Almost Every Major African Economy
Ethiopia ranks ninth at US$127.15 billion, but its growth rate makes it one of the most consequential economies in the ranking. The IMF expects Ethiopia’s real economy to expand by about 9.2 percent in 2026, the fastest rate among the continent’s major economies listed here.
If sustained, that pace can dramatically change the ranking over time. At 9 percent annual real growth, an economy roughly doubles in size in about eight years before considering inflation and exchange rate effects.
Ethiopia’s challenge is that extremely rapid domestic growth has existed alongside significant foreign exchange shortages, inflation, external debt pressures and a major currency adjustment. Those factors can suppress nominal GDP in US dollar terms even when local production is expanding rapidly.
The country therefore illustrates the opposite side of the Nigerian problem. Ethiopia can be one of Africa’s fastest growing economies without immediately becoming one of the largest in dollar terms because currency effects reduce the international value of domestic output.

articles.title: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic Opportunity, Economic Imperative or Geopolitical Gamble? - Business & Financial Times
articles.summary: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic Opportunity, Economic Imperative or Geopolitical Gamble?  Business & Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Hon. Samuel Okudzeto Abalakwa, Ghana’s Foreign Affairs Minister, announced cabinet’s approval for Ghana’s application to join the BRICS, at a joint press briefing with India’s External Affairs Minister during his visit to Accra. The Honourable Minister linked the decision to the President’s “New Economy” agenda and the desire for Ghana to chart its own path without being constrained by the conditionalities of a few international institutions. This announcement formalises a relationship that trade data has been describing for years.
The open questions are what formal membership adds, what it might cost, and how businesses should position themselves while the process plays out. The conversation is more relevant now, as Ghana transitions from a period of macroeconomic stabilisation towards one focused on investment-led growth and structural transformation.
Understanding BRICS and Why It Matters
What began in the early 2000s as an economic acronym coined to describe the fast-growing emerging economies of Brazil, Russia, India and China has evolved into one of the most influential geopolitical and economic blocs in the world. South Africa joined the grouping in 2010, transforming BRIC into BRICS and providing Africa with representation within the bloc. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE later joined, followed by Indonesia in 2025, bringing membership to 11, with Nigeria and several other countries holding partner status.
The group’s main institution is the New Development Bank (NDB), headquartered in Shanghai. The bank has approved over 120 projects worth about US$40 billion and admits new members on the condition that the founding BRICS countries' capital share never falls below 55%. One stated ambition - reducing reliance on the US Dollar - remains a key aspiration yet to be realised.
BRICS today is no longer simply a forum for emerging economies. It represents a broader vision for increasing the influence of developing nations within global governance structures. For many countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America, the appeal of BRICS lies not in replacing existing global institutions, but in creating additional options. In an increasingly uncertain global environment characterised by economic fragmentation, geopolitical competition and shifting trade dynamics, diversification has become a strategic necessity.
Why Ghana Is Looking Towards BRICS
Ghana's interest in BRICS comes at a pivotal moment in its economic journey.
Following years of economic turbulence, debt restructuring and IMF-supported reforms, the Country has made notable progress in restoring macroeconomic stability. Economic discussions are increasingly shifting from stabilisation towards growth, productivity, investment and industrialisation. Internal economic briefings and policy discussions increasingly focus on how Ghana can move from recovery to sustainable private-sector-led growth.
At the same time, the global economic environment is changing. Emerging markets are playing a larger role in global trade and investment flows, while developing countries are seeking greater influence within international institutions.
Against this backdrop, BRICS presents Ghana with an opportunity to expand its economic options.
Government officials have publicly framed the proposed membership as part of a broader strategy to diversify international partnerships and create new avenues for cooperation. This rationale aligns closely with the Country's broader ambitions around industrialisation, infrastructure development, job creation and economic transformation.
The Economic Case for Membership
The strongest arguments in favour of Ghana joining BRICS are arguably economic rather than political. Four key areas of potential benefit to Ghana have been highlighted below:
· Alignment with where Ghana's trade already goes: This is the strongest economic argument. In 2025, the UAE took 25.9% of Ghana's exports, India 16.0%, South Africa 10.3% and China 4.9%. All four are BRICS members, which means roughly 57% of Ghana's export earnings already flow to the bloc. On the import side, China remained Ghana's largest supplier at about 23% of imports in the fourth quarter of 2025. Membership could institutionalise relationships that are already central to Ghana's balance of payments, while opening additional channels for exports and investment promotion.
· Development financing options: Ghana has completed a demanding IMF programme and now engages the Fund through a Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI), a non-financing arrangement that offers technical support and policy guidance. With no IMF money on the table, access to the NDB for infrastructure financing (energy, rail, water, digital) would widen the menu of long-tenor capital at a time when Ghana needs to finance growth. These investments will be essential if the Country is to realise its ambition of becoming a competitive industrial economy.
· Industrial and technology partnerships: The visit by India’s External Affairs Minister itself showed what is on offer, with plans announced to deepen cooperation in railways, pharmaceuticals, ICT, defence, agriculture and science and technology. If Ghana uses membership to negotiate local value addition, such as gold refining, cocoa processing and pharmaceutical manufacturing, rather than simply more raw commodity exports, the growth dividend could be real.
· Negotiating leverage: Being in more rooms strengthens Ghana's hand with every partner, including the Bretton Woods institutions, on debt treatment, climate finance and conditionality, amongst others.
Lessons from Africa's BRICS Experience
To understand what BRICS membership could mean for Ghana, it is important to examine the experiences of African countries already within the bloc.
South Africa's journey offers perhaps the most relevant case study. Since joining BRICS in 2010, South Africa has used the platform to deepen trade and investment relationships, expand diplomatic influence and access development financing through the New Development Bank. The NDB's first South African loan in 2016 supported renewable energy, and the bank has since backed 13 projects there worth around US$9 billion (in current terms), including a loan of up to US$1 billion for water and sanitation infrastructure under the Municipal Infrastructure Grant programme. The lesson is that the NDB can be a meaningful infrastructure financier for a member with a strong project pipeline and capable state entities. The Country continues to benefit from this association, while simultaneously maintaining strong economic relationships with Europe and the United States.
Ethiopia, which joined in 2024, presents a cautionary story. At admission, one Ethiopian economist judged that the direct economic benefit would be modest, but that membership would improve investor perception and widen options for development finance. Ethiopian analysts have observed that the country's trade and investment ties are stronger with individual BRICS countries such as China, Saudi Arabia and India than with the bloc as a whole, and that membership has not offset the AGOA benefits and Western privileges that were lost. The Ethiopian Economics Association also warned that trading in local currencies could worsen forex constraints and complicate Dollar-based trade with other partners, recommending that Ethiopia manages it relationship with both BRICS and the West in the short run to the benefit of the country.
Perhaps the most important lesson from these experiences is that BRICS membership itself does not create economic transformation. Membership rewards countries that come with bankable projects and strong institutions, and it does not by itself replace Western market access. South Africa's gains did not emerge simply because it joined BRICS; they emerged because the country actively leveraged membership to attract investment, strengthen trade relationships and promote national economic priorities.
The challenges and considerations
While the economic opportunities are compelling, it would be naïve to assume that BRICS membership comes without risks.
· Western Economic Relationships management is an immediate risk: The European Union, United States and United Kingdom remain among Ghana's most important development partners, export destinations and sources of foreign direct investment. President Trump has threatened additional tariffs on countries that align with what he describes as the bloc's anti-American policies. Even though Ghana’s bilateral goods trade with the US is not relatively huge, it matters disproportionately for specific sectors. With AGOA renewal and trade negotiations unsettled, the timing requires careful diplomacy. Ghana's engagement with BRICS should not be interpreted as a pivot away from the West. Such a framing creates a false choice. The world's most successful middle-income economies typically pursue diversified international relationships rather than exclusive alliances. The strategic objective should be to broaden Ghana's options, not narrow them.
· Trade imbalance and import competition: Concerns have been raised on whether Ghana, as a largely import-driven economy, risks becoming a dumping ground for larger BRICS producers such as China. Trade defence and local-content policies must be reviewed to ensure Ghanaian manufacturers are not squeezed in the pursuit of deeper integration.
· Choice of membership tier: The membership option being considered is of significant strategic importance. There have been questions around why Ghana is not following Nigeria's route as a BRICS partner country rather than seeking full membership. Legislators have also asked for scrutiny of the conditions attached to BRICS-linked financing. Partner status or NDB membership alone might be an option to explore, since it delivers most of the financial benefits with less geopolitical exposure.

articles.title: Nigeria to address red tape affecting digital trade under AfCFTA - The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.summary: Nigeria to address red tape affecting digital trade under AfCFTA  The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.full_text:
Nigeria is working with the World Bank Group to identify gaps in its digital trade regulations as it seeks to align a pending digital economy bill and a planned e-commerce policy with the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Protocol on Digital Trade.
The regulatory gap analysis is part of efforts to ensure that the protocol, its annexes and Nigeria’s domestic laws and policies work together, according to the National Coordinator and Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian AfCFTA Coordination Office (NACO), Patience Okala.
Okala said Nigerian businesses had identified Ghana, Egypt, Rwanda, South Africa and Kenya as priority markets for expansion and regulators from the five countries were brought to Lagos to examine market-access requirements and identify areas where their processes could be aligned or mutually recognised.
Okala said the challenge, however, extends beyond aligning regulations. Businesses, she said, need reliable ways to verify trading partners, make and receive payments, transfer data securely and use digital systems that work across national borders.
She said Nigeria was one of three pilot countries selected for the Africa Digital Access and Public Infrastructure for Trade (ADAPT) initiative, run by the AfCFTA Secretariat and the Tony Blair Institute, alongside Egypt and Kenya. A team had been inaugurated in Nigeria to work on the initiative, which is intended to advance interoperability between digital systems and provide a basis for implementing the protocol.
Citing World Trade Organisation records, she said African exports of digitally delivered services grew by 15 per cent in 2024, which she described as the fastest growth recorded in any region. She said this growth underscored the need for appropriate regulatory arrangements, adding that the protocol’s provisions and annexes need to align with Nigeria’s existing regulatory framework for it to be fully implemented.
Chief Executive Officer, Better Than Cash Alliance, Nshuti Mbabazi, said the implementation of the protocol must move beyond written agreements to practical testing of cross-border payment arrangements.
Responding to a question about how a Nigerian seller could receive payment for goods ordered from Kenya, Mbabazi said the framework must be tested through actual transactions to identify the barriers preventing businesses from completing payments reliably. She proposed identifying a small group of traders willing to buy and sell along the Nigeria–East Africa corridor and using their transactions to test the framework. The exercise, she said, would help establish the actual obstacles to trusted electronic payments.
She said the Better Than Cash Alliance would work to activate cross-border digital trade payment proofs of concept, adding that similar work had started in East Africa and could also be undertaken between Nigeria and East African markets.
According to her, businesses should be able to access information required to register and verify their operations online without physically visiting offices. She added that trusted digital identity recognised across participating African markets would help businesses establish legitimacy and build confidence among prospective trading partners.
Drawing on her experience in Aba’s textiles, leather and manufacturing sectors, Mbabazi said digital platforms have made communication with potential customers easier, but challenges persist when businesses need to make payments or move goods across borders as affordable payment arrangements and reliable ways to track goods until delivery is needed.
Mbabazi highlighted the potential of fintech passporting, under which a company licensed in Nigeria could expand into another participating African country without repeating extensive regulatory procedures. She urged African countries to work across regional economic communities, including the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the East African Community (EAC), to establish interoperable systems that make cross-border transactions as straightforward as domestic ones.
Head of Regulatory Unit at the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), Ibukunoluwa Owa, said secure cross-border data transfers were essential to building trust among businesses trading under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), urging Nigerian operators to understand and comply with the country’s data protection requirements before expanding into other African markets. She outlined different mechanisms for obtaining approval, including an adequacy route under which the commission assesses whether a destination country provides comparable protection.
Owa identified standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules, certification mechanisms and codes of conduct as possible instruments for cross-border data transfers, subject to applicable requirements. She explained that contractual clauses could be adapted to specific transactions, while binding corporate rules could support transfers within groups of companies operating in different countries.
Owa said limited exceptions, including informed consent and contractual necessity, could apply in specific circumstances. However, she advised businesses that transferred data regularly to rely on adequacy decisions or transfer instruments rather than treating these exceptions as their principal route.
She identified digital identity, secure data transfers and regulatory convergence as important to building trust in cross-border digital trade. She said Nigeria was leading a regulatory harmonisation working group under the Network of Africa Data Protection Authorities to improve alignment of cross-border data transfer rules and make compliance easier for businesses operating across jurisdictions.
Representing the Director of e-governance services at the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Oluwatosin Lewis-Okoh, said digital trade required reliable broadband, interoperable systems and trusted identities, alongside payment and customs arrangements that supported transactions from identifying buyers and sellers to exchanging data, settling payments and processing customs documentation.
On digital identity and trust, she said businesses trading across borders need reliable ways to establish the identities of the people and organisations they trade with. She referred to changes involving public key infrastructure and the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), explaining that trusted identity systems are key to establishing confidence between buyers and sellers in different countries.
She illustrated this with the example of a Nigerian fashion entrepreneur selling to a customer in Kigali. 
For the transaction to succeed, the seller would need a verified customer identity, a payment arrangement that could settle across borders, electronic customs documentation and assurance that the customer’s personal data was protected. “If one of these links breaks, the sale breaks,” she said, stressing the need for integrated infrastructure rather than separate systems.

articles.title: Egypt seeks infrastructure financing, investment partnerships at IMF/World Bank meetings in Bangkok - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Egypt seeks infrastructure financing, investment partnerships at IMF/World Bank meetings in Bangkok  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
Egypt’s ministers meet World Bank officials, Kuwaiti counterpart and international investors as Cairo highlights economic reforms, private-sector-led growth and efforts to reduce debt burdens.
Egypt is seeking to expand investment partnerships and secure new financing for infrastructure projects as its ministers hold talks with international financial institutions, investors and regional counterparts on the sidelines of the 2026 annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group in Bangkok, Thailand.
The meetings kicked off on Monday, running through Sunday 18 October.
Minister of Planning and Economic Development Ahmed Rostom and Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty met senior World Bank officials to review Egypt’s economic performance and development priorities, while discussions with Kuwait focused on establishing a financing guarantee mechanism for Egyptian infrastructure projects in cooperation with the National Investment Bank.
The meetings come as Egypt seeks to build on economic growth, increase private-sector investment and attract financing on more competitive terms amid persistent global and regional challenges.
During a meeting with Michael Kremer, the World Bank Group’s chief economist and senior vice president for development economics, attended by both Egyptian ministers, Rostom said the economy had demonstrated resilience in the face of geopolitical tensions.
Egypt’s GDP grew by 5.1 percent in the fiscal year 2025/2026, which ended in June, while the private sector’s share of total investments rose to 57.7 percent, Rostom said.
The meeting also reviewed the implementation of the government’s economic and social development plan for the current FY2026/2027, which starts on 1 July, and the main features of the National Economic Transformation Programme, which is being prepared in line with directives from President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and builds on the country’s previous reform efforts.
In separate talks, the two ministers met Kuwaiti finance minister Yaqoub Al-Rifai to discuss practical steps to expand bilateral economic cooperation and translate investment opportunities into development projects.
The discussions focused on activating a mechanism to guarantee financing for infrastructure projects in Egypt, in coordination with the National Investment Bank, with the aim of attracting more Kuwaiti investment and supporting the country’s infrastructure and development plans.
Finance Minister Ahmed Kouchouk also held meetings with international investors and development finance institutions on the sidelines of the Bangkok meetings, presenting the government’s priorities for encouraging private-sector investment, boosting production and exports, and reducing public debt.
Speaking at a roundtable with investors from Jefferies, Kouchouk said Egypt’s economic position remained sound and attractive to investment despite global and regional challenges, adding that the government would continue implementing reforms.
He said fiscal policies were designed to support economic activity while maintaining flexibility, balance and financial discipline.
The government was pursuing several initiatives to encourage private businesses to invest, expand production and increase exports, Kouchouk said, adding that it was working with government partners and the business community to improve the investment climate through further facilitation, greater certainty and clearer policies.
He also said the government was pursuing an ambitious strategy to reduce public debt in absolute terms, as a share of GDP and in terms of its servicing burden.
Kouchouk cited recent decisions by credit rating agencies to maintain Egypt’s sovereign ratings with stable outlooks, saying the assessments reflected continued confidence in the economy. Fitch affirmed Egypt’s rating at ‘B’, while S&P Global Ratings maintained its ‘B/B’ ratings, both with stable outlooks.
The private sector is driving economic growth, supported by strong performances in manufacturing, tourism, and communications and information technology, the minister added.
In a separate meeting with Samih Shennouda, executive director and head of investment at the Africa Finance Corporation (AFC), Kouchouk discussed expanding cooperation to finance Egyptian projects in partnership with the private sector.
He said the government’s economic and fiscal priorities centred on increasing private-sector investment and its contribution to the economy, while encouraging investment in activities capable of generating higher economic returns and increasing goods and services exports.
Kouchouk described AFC as a strategic partner capable of mobilising additional private capital to support development in Egypt.
The two sides are looking to establish a new phase of bilateral cooperation, including the preparation of a joint list of priority economic activities to support sustainable growth, he said.
Egypt also aims to reach new categories of investors across a wider range of financing markets and secure funding on more competitive terms to reduce borrowing costs, Kouchouk added.
Separately, Abdelatty participated on Tuesday, 13 October, in a meeting of ministers and governors of the Group of 24 (G24), where he highlighted the resilience of the Egyptian economy despite mounting pressures on the global economy and developing countries.
Abdelatty said the current challenges also presented opportunities to reshape economic partnerships and strengthen regional integration.
Building resilience requires credible macroeconomic frameworks and international institutions that are more responsive to the needs of developing economies, he said, calling for stronger collective action and improvements to international financing mechanisms to ease the burdens facing developing countries and support sustainable development.
The foreign minister also outlined Egypt’s economic reforms aimed at strengthening stability and improving the investment climate.
He highlighted investment opportunities in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, ports, renewable energy and green hydrogen, saying these sectors could help strengthen domestic value chains, support industrialisation and create jobs.
Abdelatty further stressed the importance of stronger regional and international connectivity in energy, transport and trade, as well as deeper regional integration and the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area agreement to advance shared economic interests and development across the continent.
The annual IMF and World Bank Group meetings are being held in Bangkok from 12 to 18 October, bringing together policymakers, financial institutions, and other stakeholders to discuss global economic challenges and development priorities.

articles.title: AfCFTA Moves To Transform Africa’s Automotive Industry - News Ghana
articles.summary: AfCFTA Moves To Transform Africa’s Automotive Industry  News Ghana
articles.full_text:
…Through Investment, Local Manufacturing And Regional Value Chains
The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat has renewed its commitment to transforming Africa’s automotive industry, calling for greater investment in local manufacturing, stronger regional supply chains and increased production of vehicle components across the continent.
Speaking at the inaugural Africa Automotive Investment Forum, held on the sidelines of the Alamein Africa Business Forum in Egypt, the Secretary-General of the AfCFTA Secretariat, H.E. Wamkele Mene, emphasised the need to move beyond trade negotiations and translate agreed continental frameworks into tangible industrial development, employment and economic opportunities.
With the automotive Rules of Origin under the AfCFTA now concluded, the Secretary-General said attention must turn to implementing policies that encourage investment, expand manufacturing capacity and strengthen Africa’s participation in automotive production.
“The focus now shifts from establishing the rules to translating them into investment, production and employment,” he stated.
The Secretary-General outlined three priorities for advancing the Strategy for the African Automotive Sector under the AfCFTA framework. These include developing investment-ready projects and competitive production locations, strengthening regional supplier networks while deepening local manufacturing, and ensuring that automotive production across African markets becomes commercially viable.
A major focus of the initiative is to establish stronger connections between vehicle assembly plants and African manufacturers of essential automotive components, including tyres, glass, plastics, textiles, electronics and batteries.
Such integration is expected to create opportunities for African businesses to participate in regional production networks, increase local value addition and support the development of a competitive continental automotive industry.
The Secretary-General further underscored the importance of improving customs procedures, transit arrangements, product standards and regulatory alignment to facilitate the movement of automotive components and finished vehicles across African markets.
He also highlighted the strategic opportunity for Africa to leverage its abundant mineral resources to develop domestic processing industries, battery materials production, component manufacturing and vehicle assembly.
This approach would enable African economies to retain a greater share of the value generated from their natural resources while promoting industrial development, technological advancement and employment.
AfCFTA Secretariat Signs Strategic Automotive Partnership
In a significant development on the margins of the Forum, the AfCFTA Secretariat and the African Association of Automotive Manufacturers (AAAM) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at strengthening cooperation towards the sustainable development of Africa’s automotive industry.
The agreement was signed by H.E. Wamkele Mene, Secretary-General of the AfCFTA Secretariat, and Mr. Tarek Mosaad, President of AAAM.
The partnership establishes a framework for collaboration in implementing the Strategy for the African Automotive Sector, including automotive Rules of Origin, customs procedures, trade facilitation, regulatory standards, capacity building, supplier development, investment mobilisation and emerging automotive technologies.
It will also promote mineral beneficiation, enabling African countries to move beyond exporting raw materials towards developing higher-value manufacturing activities within the automotive industry.
Importantly, the agreement will support the development and implementation of the AfCFTA Automotive Investment Plan being advanced by the AfCFTA Secretariat in collaboration with the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank).
The initiative seeks to identify viable investment opportunities, mobilise financing and facilitate the development of integrated automotive value chains across the continent.
The inaugural Forum brought together government representatives, automotive manufacturers, suppliers, investors and development finance institutions to explore opportunities for accelerating investment and industrial partnerships under the AfCFTA.
The discussions and partnership signal a shift towards practical implementation of the continental trade agreement, with automotive manufacturing identified as an important pathway for industrialisation, economic diversification and regional integration.
By connecting Africa’s mineral resources, manufacturing capabilities, investment opportunities and expanding continental market, the AfCFTA framework offers a platform for building an increasingly integrated automotive industry.
The emerging priority is to ensure that agreed trade rules translate into functioning factories, competitive African suppliers, sustainable employment and greater participation by African enterprises in continental and global automotive value chains.

articles.title: Chinese exports to South Africa jump 29% as Trump’s trade war puts local factories under fresh pressure - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Chinese exports to South Africa jump 29% as Trump’s trade war puts local factories under fresh pressure  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Chinese shipments to South Africa rose 29% in January–August 2026, according to Bloomberg.
- Manufacturers face stronger import competition alongside longstanding domestic operating challenges.
- Official figures show South African manufacturing output fell 4.3% year-on-year in August.
- Import growth and factory weakness are connected pressures, but the data do not establish a single cause.
Shipments increased 29% compared with January–August 2025, adding to the challenges facing businesses trying to rebuild domestic production.
The consequences reach beyond trade balances. Manufacturers competing with imported finished goods must win orders while covering the costs of local production and employment.
Cheaper imports can benefit buyers, but they can also make it harder for domestic producers to maintain sales and justify investment.
According to Bloomberg’s 13 October report, the influx is affecting businesses across industrial supply chains. At cable manufacturer Alvern Cables, works director Jaycen Padiachy said the company was facing increased competition, with imports affecting its business.
Official figures show an uneven recovery
Statistics South Africa’s latest manufacturing release provides a separate measure of the sector’s difficulties.
Output fell 4.3% in August compared with a year earlier. Vehicle manufacturing, transport equipment, chemicals, food production and metals were among the divisions contributing to the decline.
Seasonally adjusted production also fell 3.1% from July. However, the broader picture was mixed: production over the three months to August was 1.1% higher than in the preceding three months, with eight of ten manufacturing divisions recording growth.
Those figures show a fragile recovery rather than uninterrupted decline. They also do not identify how much of the weakness was caused by Chinese competition.
Import competition is not the same as dumping
South Africa has already used trade-remedy investigations to examine complaints from domestic manufacturers.
In an October 2025 notice, the International Trade Administration Commission detailed a case involving certain Chinese flat-rolled steel products used in construction and manufacturing.
ArcelorMittal South Africa and SAFAL Steel alleged that the imports were undercutting prices and harming producers within the Southern African Customs Union.
ITAC reported a preliminary finding of dumping and material injury in that specific case. It did not impose provisional anti-dumping duties at that stage, citing safeguard measures already introduced.
That investigation concerns particular products and evidence. It does not establish that Chinese imports generally are being dumped.
South Africa’s two-way China challenge
The pressure comes as South Africa also seeks to expand exports to China.
Recently, South African commodities flooded the Chinese market. Greater access can support exporters, while competition from Chinese finished goods creates a different challenge for domestic factories.
The automotive industry illustrates the changing competitive landscape. Chinese brands increased their share of South Africa’s passenger-car market from 11.2% in 2024 to 16.8% in 2025, according to industry body naamsa.
Policymakers must balance access to competitively priced goods with the need to protect local industries from demonstrable harm. The 29% increase adds urgency to that debate, but it does not explain South Africa’s manufacturing problems on its own.

articles.title: ANALYSIS: Regional Trade, Economic Strategy Draw Asian and African States Closer in BRICS - Business Post Nigeria
articles.summary: ANALYSIS: Regional Trade, Economic Strategy Draw Asian and African States Closer in BRICS  Business Post Nigeria
articles.full_text:
By Professor Maurice Okoli
Perhaps, BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), with the new members and partner states, summit in New Delhi, on September 11 to13, produced a new round of significant declarations, adapting its collective policy towards an increasingly emerging architecture, while distinctively building an ‘Asian model’ of economic alliance. Under the chairmanship of India, the summit centred on creating a genuine reputation that has accumulated for nearly two decades. The timing was, particularly, notable. The most important strategic message was coined: “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability.”
Addressing the BRICS summit of leading developing nations in New Delhi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi warned that rising geopolitical tensions could increasingly affect people worldwide, and called for deepening cooperation and strengthening support across the Global South.
“The number of conflicts and tensions in the world is continuously increasing, and this is having an increasingly negative and far-reaching impact on the lives of ordinary people,” Modi said, alongside leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa.
That was one of the main messages sent across the world. Founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, BRICS has expanded to 11 members representing about half the world’s population and a significant share of global economic output. It has sought greater representation for developing countries in global institutions and promoted alternative actions to Western-dominated financial systems.
Geopolitics: Is BRICS Challenging the West?
BRICS leaders adopted the New Delhi Declaration, expressing indispensable concern relating to forging consensus over many strategic questions, backing greater use of local currencies in trade and stronger cross-border payment systems, while calling for cooperation on food security, energy, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and climate action. The declaration was a significant breakthrough, which holds competing positions on key regional and geopolitical issues, posing a complex diplomatic challenge amid ongoing conflicts and heightened geopolitical tensions. It emphasises collective support for a multipolar world order and operational and structural reforms at the United Nations, including its Security Council, as well as global financial institutions such as the World Bank (WB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The declaration demonstrated that BRICS can move together and act on multilateral economic cooperation, and its sustainability in the Global South. That makes the question whether India has used its presidency to drum home for BRICS grouping to become more capable of taking economic action, with reports indicating that India entered a particular moment with more than just diplomatic presence. For instance, during the financial year 2024-25, its total exports amounted to approximately $825 billion, with services accounting for an estimated $387 billion.
Few developing countries can match New Delhi’s economic leverage, which stems from its large domestic market, expansion of the digital economy, and sustainable growth. Despite national preferences and differences between BRICS members, it is worthy to note that India is a major provider of digital public infrastructure, and its demography plays an increasingly important role in global consumption, production, and services.
It, therefore, exemplifies that BRICS members have to build economic prosperity by opening doors. This new phase must strategically focus on broader economic leverage. And appropriately, India’s geography provides an additional layer of economic leverage, which serves as a classic example for other Asian countries.
Сorporate Economic Weight, Limited Collective Power
While BRICS’s economic weight is enormous–its ability to wield it collectively is not, some analysts argued. However, experts’ arguments closely connected to BRICS operational successes and achievements should not only be measured by whether it can pose an alternative to multinational institutions, but also whether it could make any noticeable difference, in terms of using its natural resources to increase regional trade, raise economic production and improve distribution across the Global South. Several experts portray BRICS as offering its member countries alternative pathways for channelling trade and investment that serve the collective interests of member countries–largely national development and poverty alleviation.
Meanwhile, scholars have reminded that BRICS emerged after the 2008 financial collapse and the failures of the World Trade Organization’s (WTO) Doha Round–trade negotiations aimed at reforming the international trading system in favour of Global South countries. Why would the BRICS want to take on the global governance responsibilities of the G7 members? This has been the basic question among scholars until today. It is, however, believed that reforms and greater autonomy would be a greater concern for BRICS rather than overthrowing the unravelling liberal international order.
BRICS+ Financial Architecture
The group is noticeably dominated by China, which has the largest share of the group’s GDP, accounting to about 70% of the organisation’s total. The financial architecture of BRICS is made up of the New Development Bank (NDB) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA). These components were signed into a treaty in 2014 and became active in 2015. The New Development Bank (NDB), formerly referred to as the BRICS Development Bank, is a multilateral development bank operated by the five BRICS states. It has non-members as contributors to the NDB.
The bank’s primary focus of lending is infrastructure projects, with authorised lending of up to $34 billion annually. South Africa hosts the African headquarters of the bank. The bank has a starting capital of $50 billion, with wealth increasing to $100 billion over time. Records show Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa initially contributed $10 billion each to bring the total to $50 billion. As of 2020, it had 53 projects underway worth around $15 billion. By 2025, the bank had approved more than $32 billion for 96 projects.
In 2021, Bangladesh, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates and Uruguay joined the NDB. With India’s presidency in 2026, which was estimated to be comprehensive and promising for BRICS, India has outlined its framework of priorities, as it did during its G20 presidency several years ago. In close coordination with members and partner states within the BRICS, India has ensured the balance of multifaceted interests and established mutual trust in the multipolar world system. The goal of transforming into a full-fledged international organisation must go beyond addressing current geopolitical challenges; it also requires developing effective ways of engaging in global development to reflect multipolarity. Today, collectively, BRICS comprises more than a quarter of the global economy and nearly half the world’s population.
BRICS Advocates for Reforms at Financial Institutions
Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors of BRICS countries have called for reform of global developmental financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, seeking a stronger voice for emerging market economies. “We will continue to strengthen coordination among BRICS members to make international financial institutions more representative, transparent and accountable. With the growing share of emerging market and developing economies in global output and growth, reform of global economic governance remains a consistent BRICS priority,” Finance Chiefs of BRICS countries underlined in an official joint statement.
“We continue to have serious concerns with the unilateral imposition of trade and finance-related actions, including the raising of tariffs and non-tariff measures, which distort trade and are inconsistent with World Trade Organisation rules,” the statement said. “We encourage the BRICS Payment Task Force to continue discussions, building on the ongoing work, to facilitate practical solutions for cross-border payments among BRICS countries, which are fast, low-cost, more accessible, efficient, transparent, and safe,” the statement said. While acknowledging the work done by the BRICS payment task force, the finance chiefs pushed for progress in ensuring greater interoperability of payment systems across member nations. It further noted that India will push for progress on linking digital currencies across BRICS countries.
BRICS-Africa Transiting from Diplomacy to Strategic Economy
South Africa (2010), Ethiopia and Egypt (2024), as fully-fledged BRICS members, are seemingly changing policy, which has always been strategic ambiguity, to a kind of assertive flexibility. South Africa, Ethiopia and Egypt are also positioning themselves as leading African voices for the Global South while, at the same time, maintaining relationships with competing Western powers. In principle, Africa generally collaborates with the United States and Asia-Pacific partners while striking, to a certain degree, multifaceted ties with Russia, and operates within the framework of the BRICS domain.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, and President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi of the Arab Republic of Egypt held separate conversations on the current status and future prospects for their relations, and further discussed ways of strengthening BRICS strategic partnership in politics and security, economics and finance, and cultural and humanitarian ties, while exchanging divergent views on current international and regional issues that are of common significance to global development. articles.title: Government invests R8.9 billion to restore key iron ore export corridor - South African Government News Agency
articles.summary: Government invests R8.9 billion to restore key iron ore export corridor  South African Government News Agency
articles.full_text:
Government is investing R8.9 billion to restore the 861 km Iron Ore Export Line, strengthening a critical freight corridor that links Sishen in the Northern Cape to the Port of Saldanha in the Western Cape.
“The Transnet Rail Infrastructure Manager’s (TRIM) long-term Ore Line Restoration Programme, which runs until 2030, is valued at approximately R8.9 billion and is aimed at restoring reliability, improving capacity and supporting economic growth through a safe, efficient and reliable rail network,” Minister of Transport Barbara Creecy said during a site visit to the Iron Ore Line on Monday, held as part of the annual maintenance shutdown.
Creecy said the export corridor is vital to mineral exports, economic activity and thousands of jobs across the logistics value chain.
“This corridor is therefore far more than a railway line. It is an economic artery that supports exports, industrial growth and employment across our economy.
“When this corridor performs well, mines can move their commodities efficiently, exporters can reach international markets, ports can operate more effectively and businesses across the logistics value chain can grow. It also strengthens South Africa’s position as a reliable trading partner,” Creecy said.
Intensive maintenance during shutdown
The annual maintenance shutdown, underway from 6 to 16 October, gives TRIM a dedicated window to carry out intensive work that would be difficult to complete while normal rail operations continue.
During the shutdown, teams are replacing rail and sleepers, screening ballast, replacing and maintaining turnouts, accelerating track maintenance, rehabilitating formations and installing culverts. Electrical and signalling maintenance is also underway.
“These may sound like highly technical activities, but ultimately they have a simple purpose: to build a safer, more reliable and more efficient railway.
“Safety is not separate from delivery. It is the foundation of delivery. The success of this shutdown will be measured not only by the maintenance completed, but by ensuring that every person returns home safely and that the corridor is restored to service without compromise,” the Minister said.
Funding rail and rolling stock renewal
To support the programme, government has allocated R3.4 billion through the Budget Facility for Infrastructure (BFI) over the current and next financial years.
This year, TRIM will invest approximately R2.2 billion in restorative maintenance on the Ore Corridor, including R1.5 billion funded through the BFI allocation.
Transnet’s efforts to improve operations on the line also include R1.47 billion for ore line rolling stock maintenance: R752.3 million for wagons and R721.9 million for locomotives.
Similar amounts will be allocated to rolling stock maintenance in the next financial year.
“These investments will support critical maintenance and overhaul programmes, including the 15GO and 43DGO locomotive overhaul programmes, while addressing long-standing maintenance backlogs and improving fleet availability, reliability and operational stability.
“Rail interventions are being complemented by strategic investments in the Port of Saldanha, ensuring an integrated corridor approach to restoring South Africa's iron ore export capacity,” Creecy said.
Port upgrades support export capacity
At the Port of Saldanha, the Transnet National Ports Authority (TNPA) is commissioning the Bulk Power Upgrade Project, representing a total capital investment of approximately R750 million.
The project will increase the port’s power supply, enabling Transnet Port Terminals to operate its third tippler and support higher export volumes through the port.
Jobs and opportunities for local businesses
“The benefits of a programme of this scale should not only be measured in kilometres of rail replaced or sleepers installed. We must also ask what this investment means for the communities through which this railway passes.
“For this October intervention, approximately 1,300 fixed-term contract opportunities have been created, with more than 600 indirect opportunities expected through associated economic activity,” the Minister said.
The programme also creates opportunities for small, medium and micro enterprises in civil works, track-related services, logistics, transportation, plant and equipment support, material supply, accommodation and other support services.
Larger contractors can extend these benefits through subcontracting and procurement from local enterprises.
Infrastructure investment underpins rail reform
“It is important that we view today's work within the broader context of South Africa's rail reform programme. Government has made a clear policy choice to restore rail as the backbone of our freight logistics system.
“A central component of this reform is opening the freight rail network to private train operating companies while retaining rail infrastructure in state ownership,” Creecy said.
She said establishing the Transnet Rail Infrastructure Manager had created a dedicated entity to manage and maintain the national rail network and provide access to it. The Network Statement sets out the framework through which train operating companies can gain access.
“However, open access cannot succeed through policy and regulation alone. We need infrastructure that can turn reform from policy into practical implementation.
“Train operating companies must have confidence that when they invest in locomotives, wagons, people and operations, the infrastructure on which those investments depend is progressively becoming safer, more reliable and more predictable.
“That is why maintenance interventions such as the one we are witnessing today are fundamental to rail reform. We cannot invite greater volumes onto the railway without investing in the infrastructure that must carry those volumes,” Creecy said. -SAnews.gov.za

articles.title: World Bank Commits Continued Financing for Tanzania’s Major Infrastructure and Social Projects - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: World Bank Commits Continued Financing for Tanzania’s Major Infrastructure and Social Projects  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
The World Bank has pledged to sustain its extensive financial support for Tanzania’s strategic national development agenda, targeting core energy integration, transport infrastructure, and human capital investments. The commitment aims to bolster the East African nation’s transition toward an industrialised economy while expanding essential social protection networks.
The policy endorsement emerged from bilateral talks held in Bangkok, Thailand, between Dr Ndiamé Diop, the World Bank’s Vice President for Eastern and Southern Africa, and Tanzania’s Finance Minister, Ambassador Khamis Mussa Omar. The meeting, conducted on the sidelines of the October 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group, signals continued confidence from multilateral lenders in Tanzania’s fiscal trajectory.
Targeting Core Infrastructure Corridors
During the negotiations, Dr Diop commended Tanzania’s recent economic resilience and outlined the Bank’s readiness to align its funding mechanisms with the country’s most capital-intensive domestic priorities. A primary focus of the renewed cooperation centres on Tanzania’s transport and logistics networks, which are viewed as critical catalysts for regional trade.
Ambassador Omar detailed that the collaborative financing framework will heavily support the ongoing modernisation of the Dar es Salaam Port. The port remains a vital maritime gateway not only for Tanzania but for landlocked neighbours including Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. By increasing cargo handling capacity, the government aims to establish Tanzania as the premier logistics hub in East Africa.
Complementing the maritime investments, the World Bank will continue to back the construction of both the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) and the rehabilitation of the traditional Central Railway (MGR). These rail networks are designed to seamlessly integrate with the port infrastructure, drastically reducing freight transit times and transport costs across the regional supply chain.
Energy Integration and the Regional Power Pool
Energy security formed another critical pillar of the Bangkok discussions. The World Bank pledged support for large-scale energy projects specifically designed to connect Tanzania’s national electricity grid with neighbouring Zambia. This strategic interconnector is a vital component of the broader Southern African Power Pool (SAPP).
By establishing a robust cross-border transmission network, Tanzania aims to transition from energy dependency to energy export, stabilising domestic power supply for growing industrial sectors while generating foreign exchange revenue through electricity sales to energy-deficient neighbours in the south.
| Key Strategic Projects Slated for Continued World Bank Financing |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Sector | Project Focus | Expected Economic Impact | 
|---|---|---|
| Transport Infrastructure | Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) and Central Railway (MGR) | Reduced freight transit times and enhanced cross-border regional trade | 
| Energy Integration | National grid connection with neighbouring Zambia | Stabilised domestic power supply and cross-border energy export capabilities | 
| Social Protection | Tanzania Social Action Fund (TASAF) | Direct financial cash transfers and capacity building for vulnerable rural households | 
| Maritime Logistics | Dar es Salaam Port expansion and modernisation | Increased bulk cargo handling capacity for the landlocked East African corridor | 
Human Capital and Social Protection Networks
Beyond physical infrastructure, the World Bank reasserted its commitment to financing Tanzania’s human capital development. A substantial portion of the ongoing partnership will be directed toward the Tanzania Social Action Fund (TASAF). The programme functions as the government’s primary social safety net, providing direct conditional cash transfers and public works employment to the country’s most vulnerable households.
Ambassador Omar emphasised that investments in social protection, alongside agriculture, health, and education, are prerequisites for sustainable economic growth. The strategic allocation of funds aims to ensure that the dividends of large-scale infrastructure projects ultimately translate into poverty reduction and improved public service delivery at the grassroots level.
Economic Baseline and Growth Trajectory
The World Bank’s sustained pledge arrives against a backdrop of robust macroeconomic indicators for Tanzania. According to data published by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) in mid-2026, the national economy expanded by 6.1 percent in the first quarter of the year, a marked acceleration from the 4.3 percent growth recorded during the corresponding period in 2025.
Maintaining this growth trajectory requires immense capital liquidity, far exceeding domestic revenue mobilisation capacities. The Tanzanian government has actively cultivated relationships with international financial institutions to close this funding gap without resorting to unsustainable commercial borrowing.
The successful execution of the Bangkok agreements will require stringent accountability frameworks. As the World Bank channels billions of dollars into these sectors, the Ministry of Finance faces mounting domestic pressure to ensure transparent procurement processes, rigorous project management, and timely delivery of infrastructure milestones that genuinely serve the Tanzanian public.

articles.summary: RISE Summit 2026 brings global investment leaders to Dubai as shifting capital flows reshape growth opportunities  Zawya
articles.full_text:
- ‘Capital allocation will change phenomenally – and diversification across geographies and sectors is key’ – José Manuel Barroso of Goldman Sachs
- ‘The lines between real estate and infrastructure are getting blurred…creating interesting opportunities for portfolio construction – Ludovic Subran, Allianz
UAE: As geopolitical shifts, changing trade relationships and evolving financial conditions reshape the global economic landscape, RISE Summit 2026 brought together leading investors, policymakers, developers and industry decision-makers at Dubai World Trade Centre today to examine where capital is moving and where the next phase of global growth could emerge.
Held under the theme ‘Recharging Momentum in Global Economies,’ the Summit explored how changing investment priorities are influencing global markets, infrastructure, cities and real estate, alongside the future experience economy spanning hospitality, tourism and new models of urban growth.
The UAE’s broader economic transformation was also a central theme of the Summit. Speaking during ‘From Resilience to Opportunity in a Realigning World,’ H.E. Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri, UAE Minister of Economy and Tourism, highlighted the country’s focus on building a more productive economy.
His Excellency said: “When you ask about 2027, we're not going to come back to the same economy. We're going to have a different economy in 2027, a more productive economy.”
Global Leaders Series examines international forces sharping investment landscape
The Summit opened with its Global Leaders Series, examining the changing dynamics of international capital and the forces reshaping long-term investment decisions. In ‘The Great Capital Shift,’ José Manuel Barroso, Chairman of International Advisors at Goldman Sachs and former President of the European Commission, examined how geopolitical and economic realignment is changing perceptions of where capital can be deployed safely and productively, and which markets are emerging as beneficiaries of this shift.
This was followed by Ludovic Subran, Group Chief Investment Officer and Chief Economist at Allianz, who addressed the implications of the changing interest-rate environment for institutional investors in ‘Long-Term Capital in a Higher-Rate World’, including the evolving balance between fixed income, real estate, infrastructure and private markets.
Highlighting the need for investors to adapt to a rapidly evolving global landscape, Barroso said: “We are witnessing a fundamental change. This is not only geopolitical; it is also a scientific and technological revolution, and the way we allocate capital is going to change phenomenally. Long-term investors need to think strategically about what will change markets in the years ahead – energy, infrastructure, technology and defence. Don’t pay any price for growth, keep some liquidity and, above all, diversify – geographically and across sectors. For me, that is the key.”
On the Gulf’s position within shifting global capital flows, Barroso added: “Global competition is going to continue. The US will remain the central part of the world economy because of the pre-eminence of the dollar, its advances in innovation and science and its geopolitical power. At the same time, global investors will not want to be so heavily exposed to the US, so there will be diversification. The Gulf has been wise in keeping its options open, using its centrality to play an articulation role between new destinations for investment.”
Looking beyond the AI investment boom
Turning to the global growth outlook, Subran highlighted the increasing influence of AI investment on economic momentum, while warning of growing caution across the wider economy. With data-centre investment and AI-related capital expenditure continuing to underpin growth, he questioned what could emerge as the next major economic driver as the current cycle eventually begins to shift.
Subran said: “My main concern is whether the US can sustain the momentum we have seen so far with what is coming in 2027. Global trade is in recession this year if you take out AI, which shows how much the AI economy and data-centre capex are driving global and US growth. At some point that will inflect, and we need to understand what comes next. Outside AI, firms are already very cautious about the future and about making their next investment.”
Against this higher-rate backdrop, Subran also pointed to a changing role for real assets within institutional portfolios, as the boundaries between real estate, infrastructure and technology become increasingly blurred.
He added: “Real estate is really morphing into something much more complicated. The lines between real estate and infrastructure are getting blurred, particularly across logistics and warehousing, creating interesting opportunities for portfolio construction.”
Deepening global appeal through local strength
Dubai’s own development trajectory formed another major strand of discussion. Mohamed Alabbar, Founder and Managing Director of Emaar Properties, examined the role of long-term conviction in city-building and why major development can continue through changing market cycles, while H.E. Issam Kazim, CEO of Dubai Corporation for Tourism and Commerce Marketing (DTCM) explored the economic architecture underpinning Dubai’s resilience and the next phase of growth under the D33 Economic Agenda.
Pointing to Dubai’s established strengths across multiple sectors, Kazim highlighted how the D33 agenda is building on existing foundations to deepen the city’s appeal to international businesses and investors, supported by its connectivity to global markets.
Kazim said: “When we started our D33 strategy, we focused on industries including logistics, manufacturing, financial services and tourism. None of these were new industries for us; we were already strong in them, but perhaps we were not as vocal about them. Today, we are doubling down on those strengths. Companies establish their regional headquarters in Dubai not simply for the four million residents here, but because of the global population and markets they can reach from Dubai.”
Tourism remains central to this proposition, with Kazim emphasising the value of attracting visitors who develop a lasting relationship with the city and become advocates for Dubai beyond their initial stay.
He added: “For me, the biggest value is quality rather than quantity. The quality visitors who come to Dubai become genuine advocates of the city because they understand the value Dubai adds. Around 25% of our visitors are repeat visitors within 12 months. That is a significant number, and it demonstrates the kind of relationship people develop with Dubai after experiencing the city.”
Beyond the macroeconomic outlook, RISE Summit examined how changing investment priorities are translating into opportunities across the built environment and the infrastructure needed to support future economic growth.
Across the programme, RISE Summit 2026 highlighted a changing investment environment in which capital remains available, but investors are becoming increasingly selective about markets, assets and partnerships. Discussions heard by over 500 delegates pointed to economic resilience, infrastructure capacity, regulatory clarity and access to long-term growth as increasingly important factors shaping global investment decisions.
By connecting institutional investors, sovereign capital, private equity, family offices, policymakers, developers and project owners, RISE Summit provides a platform for senior decision-makers to examine how global economic change is translating into new opportunities across markets, infrastructure, cities and real estate.
About RISE Summit 2026
RISE Summit 2026 is a high-level platform connecting institutional investors, sovereign funds, private equity firms, pension funds, family offices and global capital with governments, developers and project owners across real estate, infrastructure, hospitality, urban development and emerging investment sectors. The Summit provides a forum for senior decision-makers to examine global investment trends, identify cross-border opportunities and build partnerships around the future of cities and economies.
