articles.full_text:
Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay hit out at Donald Trump's "illegal" sanctions against the International Criminal Court, saying the US president needed a lesson in international law.
Pillay also said it was no coincidence the US sanctions on the ICC were announced just hours after her Nobel, as a "reaction to the fact that the award was not given to President Trump."
Asked what her message was for Trump, the 85-year-old judge told AFP: "Call in your legal advisors to explain to you what international law is."
"He should call in his advisors to tell him why we say that it is unlawful for him to interfere with an independent international court."
On Friday, the US announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.
Trump's administration has vowed to dismantle the court "brick-by-brick", furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza.
Pillay noted that previous US administrations had welcomed an ICC arrest warrant against Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying, "that's selective, that's double standards, and that's wrong."
The sanctions, which will hit the court's technology and banking operations, take effect in six months and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten has urged talks with Washington during that time to discuss reforms to the court, based in The Hague.
But Pillay said the idea of reforms to the ICC was "euphemistic", adding that what Trump wanted was "an undertaking that they won't pursue investigations of US citizens."
"You can't do that, because you can't have double standards. You can't selectively pursue one lot of people and not the other," Pillay told AFP.
"It will be such a bad, dangerous precedent."
Pillay also hit back at Israeli officials who reacted with outrage to her Nobel, after she headed the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry (COI), which found last year that genocide was occurring in Gaza.
Netanyahu called her a "bigot" while Israel's foreign ministry said Nazi propagandist Joseph Goebbels must be "applauding from hell" at her award.
"I think it's very hurtful and insulting," said Pillay.
"Goebbels had blood on his hands....responsible for the death of thousands of people. Not only Jews, but people of colour like me," she added.
She acknowledged there was little political appetite to arrest Netanyahu to face the ICC accusations, which he furiously denies.
"But all my life I've seen people get around difficulties, so I'm confident that it will happen," she said, asked if Netanyahu was ever likely to appear in the ICC dock.
Pillay said she was still digesting the news that she had won. She found it difficult to believe at first "because they give their awards to very few women -- gross inequality in the practice so far."
At 85, she frets she will be unable to travel far and wide to sing the praises of international justice with the amplified voice of a Nobel Peace Prize winner.
"I think that age will constrain me somewhat. I can't be as active as I used to," she said, noting that she visited 79 countries when she was UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
She said she was consulting people about how best to spend the 12 million Swedish krone prize ($1.2 million) but hinted some of it might be invested in her native South Africa.
"Africa is suffering. South Africa is suffering. It's very difficult to raise funds there," she said.
"The University of KwaZulu-Natal has set up a unit in my name, so I'll begin to have discussions with them. I believe in education for children and the youth."

articles.title: Zambia orders Konkola Copper Mines to remediate Kafue River pollution after tailings infrastructure failure - Africa Sustainability Matters
articles.summary: Zambia orders Konkola Copper Mines to remediate Kafue River pollution after tailings infrastructure failure  Africa Sustainability Matters
articles.full_text:
Zambia’s environmental authorities have ordered Konkola Copper Mines (KCM) to stop effluent discharges, remove visible tailings and assess damaged infrastructure after a pollution incident affected the Chingola and Mushishima streams and the Kafue River on 28 September, raising renewed concerns over mining operations, water security and environmental oversight in the country’s Copperbelt. In a statement issued on 1 October, the Zambia Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA) said the incident followed a reported leak at the Nchanga Mine Tailings Leach Plant and an overflow from a Pollution Control Dam.
According to ZEMA, inspectors from the agency, Mulonga Water Supply and Sanitation Company and KCM confirmed that pollutants had entered the affected waterways. The company had repaired the leak and contained the dam overflow by the time of inspection. However, preliminary laboratory tests found elevated turbidity and conductivity where the Mushishima Stream meets the Kafue River. The agency said the pH level was within acceptable limits, while further analysis for heavy metals and acidity remained pending.
The distinction between preliminary findings and confirmed contamination levels is important. Turbidity and conductivity can indicate changes in water quality, but they do not by themselves establish the concentration of specific toxic substances or the full extent of ecological damage. The additional laboratory results will be important in determining the risks to aquatic ecosystems, downstream water users and other activities dependent on the river.
Under the Environmental Management Act, Zambia’s Ministry of Green Economy and Environment issued an Environmental Restoration Order directing KCM to cease effluent discharge from the Tailings Leach Plant, remove visible tailings from affected areas and assess the integrity of pollution-control dams, tailings pipelines, decant systems and related infrastructure. The order also requires a full environmental impact assessment of the incident, followed by cleanup and remediation of affected environments and water bodies.
The government has separately issued a Cost Order requiring KCM to pay for laboratory analysis and related costs under the polluter-pays principle. According to ZEMA, the company is also expected to cover the costs of continued weekly water monitoring. The ministry said it was consulting stakeholders on appropriate penalties under the law, meaning that the final sanctions had not been established in the statement.
The response places operational controls and regulatory enforcement at the centre of the incident. Tailings infrastructure and pollution-control systems are designed to manage mining waste and prevent contaminated material from reaching surrounding land and water. When pipes leak or containment systems overflow, the consequences can extend beyond a mine’s boundary, potentially affecting water treatment, household supply, farming and aquatic habitats. The requirement for integrity assessments across related infrastructure also suggests that authorities want the investigation to look beyond the immediate failure.
For communities in Zambia’s Copperbelt, the quality and reliability of water supplies are directly connected to public health, household costs and economic activity. ZEMA said affected communities had been supplied with water through Mulonga Water Supply and Sanitation Company. That intervention provides an immediate response, but its adequacy over time will depend on the results of ongoing monitoring, the duration of any restrictions and whether the affected water sources can be safely used again.
The Kafue River is particularly significant because it supports multiple users and economic activities in Zambia. Water quality along the river system matters not only for communities near mining operations but also for downstream users, including agriculture, industry and water utilities. A pollution incident can therefore create costs that extend well beyond the operator, particularly if water treatment becomes more difficult or alternative supplies must be maintained.
The case also comes against a broader backdrop of environmental risks associated with mining-intensive economies. Copper is important to electricity networks, renewable energy systems, electric vehicles and other technologies associated with the global energy transition. Demand for the metal creates opportunities for Zambia, one of Africa’s major copper producers, to earn export revenues, attract investment and expand industrial activity. Yet the economic value of mineral production depends in part on the ability of governments and companies to manage waste, protect water resources and maintain public confidence in mining regulation.
For Zambia, the policy challenge is not simply to expand copper output, but to ensure that production does not impose unmanaged costs on communities and public infrastructure. Where environmental damage affects shared water sources, the costs of monitoring, treatment and remediation can fall across institutions and users unless responsibility is clearly assigned and enforced. Requiring the operator to fund testing and cleanup is one mechanism for preventing those costs from being transferred to the public, although its effectiveness depends on enforcement and verified remediation.
The incident also raises questions about preventive maintenance and environmental risk management. The reported leak and dam overflow point to the importance of routine inspections, infrastructure integrity testing, emergency response procedures and reliable monitoring systems. ZEMA’s order requires assessments of multiple components of the mine’s pollution-control infrastructure, which could help establish whether the incident was isolated or reflects wider weaknesses. The findings have not yet been published, and it would be premature to draw conclusions about the underlying cause beyond the reported failure.
For investors and lenders, environmental compliance is increasingly relevant to the operational and financial risks of mining assets. Pollution incidents can lead to remediation expenditure, regulatory penalties, disruption, reputational damage and potential disputes with affected communities. Clear disclosure and timely corrective action can help establish whether a company is managing these risks effectively, while uncertainty over contamination and cleanup can complicate assessments of long-term operating costs.
The next phase will depend on the outstanding laboratory results, the scope of the environmental assessment and the effectiveness of remediation. Continued monitoring by ZEMA, the Minerals Regulation Commission, the Water Resources Management Authority and other agencies will be important in establishing whether water quality recovers and whether the affected infrastructure meets required standards. The government has said it will provide further updates.
The Kafue incident underscores a wider issue for African resource-producing economies: mineral revenues and investment must be assessed alongside the quality of environmental governance that supports them. As demand for copper grows, Zambia’s ability to enforce pollution controls, hold operators responsible and protect shared water resources will remain central to the long-term economic value of its mining sector.

articles.title: Ghana's BRICS Ambitions: Why Development Must Begin at Home - Modern Ghana
articles.summary: Ghana's BRICS Ambitions: Why Development Must Begin at Home  Modern Ghana
articles.full_text:
Ghana's decision to seek closer relations with BRICS has opened an important debate about our economic future and place in the world. On 6 October 2026, Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa announced that Cabinet had approved Ghana's intention to join BRICS. He later clarified that Ghana would initially seek partner-country status rather than full membership.
Some see this as an opportunity to reduce Ghana's dependence on Western countries and international financial institutions. Others fear that we may simply replace one form of dependency with another, this time involving China, Russia and other emerging powers.
Both arguments deserve attention. The real question is whether closer cooperation with BRICS will strengthen our economy, create jobs and improve the lives of ordinary Ghanaians.
What can Ghana gain from BRICS?
BRICS brings together major emerging economies, including Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. The group has expanded to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia. Its members seek greater influence in international economic affairs and reforms of institutions such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.
For Ghana, closer cooperation could provide opportunities for trade, investment, technology and development finance. China and India are already important economic partners, while Brazil offers useful experience in agriculture and industrial development. Ghana could also explore financing opportunities through the BRICS New Development Bank, although partner status does not guarantee access to its resources.
Another possible benefit is greater diplomatic flexibility. Ghana could strengthen relations with emerging economies without abandoning its traditional Western partners. Having more partners may improve our negotiating position and reduce excessive dependence on any single country or institution. However, these benefits depend on the agreements Ghana negotiates and whether they serve our national interests.
Are we replacing one dependency with another?
One of the strongest criticisms of Ghana's proposed relationship with BRICS concerns economic dependency. Since independence, Ghana has continued to export raw materials while importing expensive finished products. We export cocoa but import chocolate. We export minerals but lack sufficient industries to transform them into finished goods.
If Ghana continues exporting raw materials to China and other BRICS countries while importing their manufactured products, what has fundamentally changed?
This concern recalls Kwame Nkrumah's warning about neo-colonialism. Political independence does not necessarily mean economic independence. A country can have its own government and flag while remaining dependent on foreign capital, technology and markets.
However, trading with powerful countries is not necessarily a new form of colonialism. Foreign investment and international cooperation can support development when agreements are fair and local industries benefit. The key question is whether Ghana will use these relationships to build productive capacity or continue supplying raw materials to more powerful economies.
Why not strengthen African integration first?
Perhaps the most important criticism concerns Africa's unfinished integration agenda. Ghana is already a member of ECOWAS and the African Union. We also host the Secretariat of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) in Accra. Yet trade between African countries remains difficult because of poor infrastructure, border delays, unnecessary checks and other barriers.
Travelling by road from Ghana through Togo and Benin to Nigeria can be frustrating. Traders face delays and additional costs that make regional business unnecessarily difficult. Why are we enthusiastic about joining international economic groupings when we have not fully addressed the barriers preventing Africans from trading freely among themselves?
This is a legitimate question posed by some critics. However, Ghana does not necessarily have to choose between BRICS and African integration. The two can complement each other if international partnerships support African industries, infrastructure and regional trade. Greater African economic integration, including closer monetary cooperation, should remain central to our development agenda.
Can Ghanaian industries compete?
China and India have large manufacturing industries and technological advantages. Ghanaian businesses, meanwhile, struggle with high production costs, expensive credit and competition from imported goods.
Closer relations with these economies could bring affordable machinery, technology and investment. However, local manufacturers could face greater pressure if Ghana fails to strengthen its industries. BRICS is not a free trade area, and partner status does not automatically remove Ghana's trade protections.
Ghana needs affordable electricity, better infrastructure, access to finance, skilled workers and incentives for local processing of raw materials. We must also negotiate agreements that encourage technology transfer and employment opportunities. Without these reforms, changing our trading partners will not transform our economy.
What about security?
Security is another concern, particularly given the threat of violent extremism in the Sahel and parts of West Africa. Some BRICS countries have significant military and technological resources that could support Ghana's security efforts. However, their political interests and approaches to regional conflicts differ considerably.
BRICS is not a collective security organisation. Ghana should therefore not assume that closer relations will automatically strengthen national security. Cooperation with neighbouring countries, ECOWAS and the African Union remains essential, alongside addressing poverty, exclusion and local conflicts that can contribute to insecurity.
Ghana must put its interests first
Foreign Minister Ablakwa has argued that closer relations with BRICS will provide Ghana with more options rather than replace its traditional partners. This distinction is important. Ghana should maintain productive relations with Western countries while exploring opportunities with emerging economies.
But having more partners does not automatically guarantee greater independence. We must ask what Ghana stands to gain in practical terms. Will these relationships create jobs, improve technology, strengthen local industries and increase the value of our exports? Will Ghanaian businesses gain meaningful access to new markets? These questions should guide our engagement with BRICS, not political enthusiasm or opposition to Western influence.
Development must begin at home
The debate about BRICS should not become another ideological struggle between East and West. Ghana's development challenges cannot be solved simply by changing its international partners.
BRICS offers possible opportunities for investment, trade, technology and greater international influence. However, risks of continued economic dependency remain if Ghana does not strengthen its domestic industries and institutions.
Nkrumah's warnings about neo-colonialism remain relevant. Genuine economic independence requires more than rejecting Western influence. It requires productive industries, strong institutions, skilled workers and fair international agreements.
The central question is whether Ghana can use these new opportunities to strengthen its economy, reduce dependency and engage its international partners on more equal terms.
Changing our international partners will not, by itself, change our economy's structure. That transformation must begin at home.
Acknowledgement
I wish to acknowledge my friend, Theophilus Sewornu Dogbeten, Head of the Analytical, Control, and Research & Development (R&D) Department at The Hospital Pharmacies Enterprise in Oslo, Norway, for an insightful discussion on Ghana's proposed relationship with BRICS. His emphasis that meaningful development in Ghana and Africa must begin at home helped sharpen the central argument of this article.

articles.title: Germany is planning major investments in rail infrastructure by 2030 - Railway PRO
articles.summary: Germany is planning major investments in rail infrastructure by 2030  Railway PRO
articles.full_text:
Germany is introducing an integrated approach to rail infrastructure development, bringing together in a single document construction and expansion projects, line electrification, corridor rehabilitation, station modernisation and noise reduction measures.
The federal ‘Infraplan 2026’ plan, covering the period 2026–2030, aims to better align long-term objectives with specific projects and funding, against a backdrop where infrastructure-related delays continue to affect the network’s performance.
The document sets out individual projects, estimated costs and implementation deadlines, alongside indicators for assessing results. The plan provides a framework for railway infrastructure projects spanning a five-year period and will be updated annually.
This comprehensive programme was launched on 6 October by Ulrich Lange, Parliamentary State Secretary at the Federal Ministry of Transport (BMV), and Philipp Nagl, CEO of DB InfraGO.
“I travel a lot by train and I know that, ultimately, what matters to people is whether the train runs reliably. And our infrastructure policy must be assessed against this criterion. That is why, with Infraplan, we are no longer looking just at individual rail projects and programmes, but at the entire network,” said Ulrich Lange.
702 km of railway corridors scheduled for refurbishment
This year’s plan provides for the refurbishment of 702 km of infrastructure on railway corridors, including 271 km on the Hamburg–Berlin route, with work due to be completed in June. This work continues the programme of major improvements carried out in previous years. In 2024, the 74 km Riedbahn section between Frankfurt and Mannheim was fully upgraded, and in 2025 work was carried out on the 73 km Emmerich–Oberhausen line.
For the period 2027–2030, this edition of the Infraplan does not set annual targets for corridor modernisation, as the programme’s strategy is currently under review. Consequently, the total number of kilometres to be upgraded relates not only to the plans for 2026 but may also be included in next year’s railway infrastructure modernisation plan. For example, it includes the project to modernise the Berlin–Hanover high-speed line, which began on 2 October and is expected to be completed by the end of 2027.
The pressure on Germany’s rail infrastructure is reflected in the trend in delays. The time lost daily due to infrastructure issues has risen from 11,843 minutes (i.e. eight and a half days) in 2020 to 28,820 minutes (i.e. over 20 days) in 2025. A figure of 28,800 minutes per day (20 days) is projected for 2026, whilst the target for 2029 and 2030 is to reduce this to 25,600 minutes per day (17 days, 18 hours and 40 minutes).
At the same time, 14 construction and expansion projects are planned, which are due to come into operation between 2026 and 2030. Among the projects scheduled for 2026 are the first section of the Karlsruhe–Offenburg–Freiburg–Basel corridor and the first section of the S13 line in the Cologne region, between Troisdorf and Bonn-Beuel.
The list also includes the doubling of the Lübbenau–Cottbus line, projects on the Angermünde–Polish border, Lübeck–Schwerin and Cologne–Aachen routes, as well as works at the Hamburg and Munich railway junctions.
Tens of billions of EUR for projects at various stages of implementation
According to the plan, there is a general category where projects at various stages of implementation are included under the ‘infrastructure requirements plan’ (Bedarfsplan). This category comprises projects involving both electrification works and ETCS implementation projects.
Category A, comprising projects currently under construction and/or with planning permission already granted, includes 38 projects with a total estimated value of approximately EUR 36 billion. These projects are due for completion between 2026 and 2030, whilst some of them will extend beyond this timeframe, with completion scheduled by 2044. One example is the project to modernise the Cologne–Düsseldorf–Dortmund/Münster corridor, known as the Rhein-Ruhr-Express (RRX), which aims to reduce severe congestion by developing a high-capacity rail corridor capable of supporting train services at 15-minute intervals.
Other rail infrastructure projects in Germany are at the design stage and in the process of obtaining the necessary approvals and authorisations for implementation (listed under category B). In this regard, the plan includes 40 projects estimated to cost nearly EUR 44 billion.
As for projects at the preliminary planning stage, there are 71 such projects (category C), with no mention of the investment required for each project. In addition, there are 34 projects at the initial assessment stage – again, with no mention of their costs.
Apart from the Bedarfsplan projects, there is also a general category known as GVFG, namely the German public transport infrastructure funding programme, which includes 83 projects totalling over EUR 28 billion, including electrification works. Here, the projects are grouped according to their status within the programme.
Category A comprises 42 projects, with a total estimated value of over EUR 18 billion. These have been definitively included in the programme on the basis of verified funding applications. Category C comprises 41 projects, with a total estimated value of over EUR 10 billion. In this case, inclusion is conditional, being based on the registration of the projects and the documentation required by the programme, subject to the agreement of the relevant federal state.
Reducing dependence on diesel traction through electrification
The electrification of the network is progressing gradually, with the Infrastructure Plan including eight projects. The proportion of electrified lines has risen from 61.2 per cent in 2020 to 62.7 per cent in 2025, and the target for 2030 is 63.7 per cent.
Key projects include the electrification of the Hochrheinbahn line, estimated at EUR 372 million, with completion scheduled for 2027, and the electrification of the Eifelstrecke in Rhineland-Palatinate, estimated at around EUR 600 million, with works due to be completed in 2028.
For the Eifel lines affected by flooding in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, the document indicates a cost of EUR 502 million, with no set completion date. Other investments include the extension and electrification of the Niddertalbahn line in the state of Hesse, with an estimated cost of EUR 318 million and a completion date of 2030.
In the Munich region, the first phase of the S-Bahn project to Wasserburg involves the electrification of the Ebersberg–Wasserburg section, at a cost of EUR 37 million, with completion scheduled for 2029.
The document also includes works on the Hürth–Kalscheuren–Euskirchen–Nettersheim–Ehrang, Euskirchen–Bad Münstereifel and Bonn–Euskirchen lines, as well as on sections of the Berlin–Cottbus–Weißwasser–Görlitz and Hanover–Berlin routes.
The figures presented relate to individual projects and do not constitute a total of investments in electrification, nor do they indicate that all works will be completed within the same timeframe.
Station modernisation and noise reduction, with annual targets
Infraplan 2026 includes specific indicators for stations and for measures to protect against rail noise. In 2025, 237 stations met the agreed standards for buildings and facilities. For 2026–2030, the target is for an average of a further 100 stations per year to meet these standards.
As regards noise reduction, measures are planned for 55 km of infrastructure in 2026. A target of 46 km is set for each year of the period 2027–2030.
The plan also includes suburban and regional transport projects. For the S-Bahn S4 line between Hamburg, Ahrensburg and Bad Oldesloe, investments of EUR 591 million from the city-state of Hamburg and EUR 253 million from the state of Schleswig-Holstein are mentioned. The extension of the S11 line in the Cologne region is estimated at EUR 854 million, although the opening date is not specified in the document.
Another major project is the second S-Bahn tunnel in Munich, for which the table indicates a value of EUR 7.33 billion in Category A, with commissioning planned for 2035. The project also appears in a conditional funding category, with a different value; the two sums should not be added together, as they do not represent separate projects.
The costs of regional projects are based on data provided by the federal states and have not been fully validated by the federal government. Infraplan warns that the figures are not directly comparable, as the calculation bases differ and do not in all cases include inflation or subsequent cost increases.
ETCS: the plan does not yet set a target for 2030
Although digitalisation is important for increasing the network’s capacity and reliability, Infraplan 2026 includes ETCS projects but does not set a quantitative target for the system’s implementation by 2030, nor does it present a separate list of digitalisation measures for this period. This is because the document explains that the federal digitalisation strategy and the new performance agreement for DB InfraGO had not yet been finalised.
The data presented shows that, in 2025, ETCS was installed on 683 km of the DB InfraGO network, equivalent to approximately 2 per cent of the network assessed. On the core TEN-T network, the system covered 594 km, or 5.8 per cent.
These figures describe the current situation and do not represent a roll-out target for 2030. Another important step is the systematic integration of the 2035 target network into the Infraplan. The main results of the process of defining this network are expected in early 2027, and its alignment with the federal plan is scheduled for the 2027 edition.

articles.title: Africa’s Infrastructure Financing Gap Gets Private Credit Bridge - Global Finance Magazine
articles.summary: Africa’s Infrastructure Financing Gap Gets Private Credit Bridge  Global Finance Magazine
articles.full_text:
With bank lending slowing, private credit is stepping in to fund Africa’s infrastructure deficit.
This article appears in the October issue of Global Finance Magazine.
Nascent private credit inflows are helping African countries and the private sector to plug infrastructure financing gaps, with energy, logistics and digital connectivity projects such as telecoms and fiber-optic internet attracting financing from this category of debt capital.
Africa’s infrastructure bottlenecks deter investors while national budgets often overlook key infrastructure funding requirements. The Southern Africa Venture Capital Association’s 2025 report notes that “private credit and infrastructure are gaining traction” across Africa in response to the region’s evolving capital needs and development priorities.
This comes at a time when development financiers and traditional lenders such as banks are increasingly throttling capital flows. Private credit is also emerging as the “most favoured strategy” for African private equity firms seeking investment diversification, the SAVCA report noted.
With a large mismatch in Africa’s infrastructure financing needs and capabilities, the burden and opportunities related to financing infrastructure development in Africa have clearly fallen on private credit investors.
“We are in exciting times for private credit in Africa. As the African continent’s financing needs continue to grow, private credit is playing an increasingly important role in providing capital to midsized corporates and supporting critical infrastructure development,” Sanaa Tabani, Standard Chartered Bank’s head of Loan Syndicate for Africa, told Global Finance in an interview.
In its 2026 State of Africa’s Infrastructure Report, the Africa Finance Corp. observed that the more than $1 trillion in assets held by nonbanking private capital institutions such as pension and insurance funds could be used as private capital to boost infrastructure development.
Standard Chartered was, however, “seeing rising investor interest in African debt opportunities, driven by growing needs” for infrastructure development.
Key Private Credit Deals for Africa
Private credit is not just flowing into critical infrastructure needs such as power, rail, ports and housing but is also providing crucial financing cover for corporate infrastructure requirements.
For example, Ninety One announced the final close for its Africa Credit Opportunities Fund 3, which raised $404 million.
Earlier, the IFC announced a $20 million investment into the Africa50 Infrastructure Acceleration Fund to finance digital infrastructure, renewable power and energy, transportation, logistics and water as well as sanitation projects across the continent.
This year’s round added to the fund’s first close that secured $222.5 million in commitments from investors that include 16 institutional financiers.
For Alain Ebobissé, CEO of Africa50 Group, the attractiveness of Africa infrastructure funds to private credit financiers reflects strong support from African institutional investors.
“This achievement is a testament to the increasing role that African institutional investors are playing in financing the real economy and unlocking Africa’s potential. The Africa50 Group plans to mobilize further private sector capital from Africa and globally into African infrastructure,” he said.
Ninety One shares the same sentiment. It said its own $404 million close had exhibited continued investor demand for private credit strategies and financing for businesses and infrastructure across the African continent among other emerging markets.
“We continue to see a significant financing gap for high-quality businesses and infrastructure projects across Africa and other emerging markets. This creates attractive opportunities for experienced lenders with deep local origination capabilities,” said Nathaniel Micklem, Ninety One’s co-head of emerging market alternative credit.
Significant Infrastructure Funding Needs
In any case, “Africa’s infrastructure funding needs are significant,” and investor appetite remains strong, with private credit having an increasingly important role to play in bridging that gap, said Pazani Vaitilingon, chief commercial officer for Africa, India, and the Middle East at IQ-EQ.
According to the World Bank’s Africa Pulse report, foundational infrastructure in Africa ranging from transport networks to general-purpose technologies like energy and digital systems is indispensable for unlocking growth across productive sectors.
However, with most African countries, from Zimbabwe, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia to Nigeria, Ivory Coast and Libya, among others, frequently experiencing electricity deficits, private capital is expected to significantly contribute to strengthening national and micro power grids and expanding mobile connectivity in less-covered areas.
There is also an alluring investment case for renewable energy for corporates. Big miners and telecom operators in Africa are seeking capital for solar power plants to sustain operations.
The Africa Pulse report notes that constrained access to power supply remains a top barrier for African businesses. To help plug connectivity gaps, the Emerging Africa and Asia Infrastructure Fund (EAAIF) in August deployed a $32.8 million senior secured loan to Eastcastle Infrastructure DRC (operating in the Democratic Republic of Congo) to boost its mobile tower base stations.
The EAAIF loan is part of a larger $179 million upsized facility for the tower company’s operations in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
BluePeak Private Capital Fund II also recently made a $12 million investment into Monty Mobile International, which offers digital connectivity solutions across Africa to support its growth.
It decided on the investment as Monty operates “essential digital infrastructure with a scalable, asset-light business model and deep relationships with mobile network operators across Africa,” said Fulton Shiundu, a partner at BluePeak Private Capital.
Investors Attain Sophisticated Understanding of Africa
Private credit investors focused on Africa have developed a more sophisticated understanding of Africa’s risk profile and opportunities. Private credit investors are also increasingly attracted by Africa’s compelling risk-adjusted returns relative to other markets.
“This growing pool of private capital is creating new funding avenues for borrowers seeking to diversify their sources of financing,” Tabani added.
Standard Chartered said it was in a position to “connect borrowers with investors,” while financial institution Investec is seeing opportunities for private credit in South Africa’s inefficient rail and port infrastructure, which is blocking export growth, investment flows and output.
“Infrastructure is starting to emerge not just as a public policy priority, but as an investable asset class,” said Ayan Ghosh, head of cross-asset investment strategy at Investec.
Nonetheless, private capital flows around Africa remain low compared to other regions, said Felix Boadi Missah, a finance and investments expert based in Ghana. He said Africa accounts for less than 1% of the global $3 trillion private credit purse, although the continent is in a growth mode with deal volumes for 2025 up by 8%.
But thanks to the $600 million attracted by Africa in private debt investment values for the first half of 2026, motorways, mobile towers, power plants and digital connectivity systems are shaping up across Africa.
Tawanda Karombo is a contributing writer based in Zimbabwe.

articles.title: Israeli technology turns on the tap for another SA village - South African Jewish Report
articles.summary: Israeli technology turns on the tap for another SA village  South African Jewish Report
articles.full_text:
On Sunday, 11 October, the 228th village in South Africa received running water due to Sivan Yaari and Innovation: Africa, a non-profit organisation that brings Israeli technology to rural African communities.
The organisation has so far brought water to 1 487 villages across the continent.
For generations, women in a northern KwaZulu-Natal village walked down a steep hill several times a day to collect water from an open, contaminated source. Now, a tap of clean water has opened up new possibilities for more than 3 000 people.
On Sunday, Innovation: Africa opened a solar-powered water system in Okledeni, near Nongoma, funded by The Victor Daitz Foundation.
Yaari, the organisation’s founder and chief executive, said the event brought together community members, royalty, and traditional and local government leaders to celebrate access to clean water. During the ceremony, one of the new taps was turned on, prompting great joy among the Okledeni community.
The project involved finding water at a depth of 150m, with a flow rate of 2.1 litres a second. More than 3km of piping was installed to supply clean water to 11 taps around the village.
“Before the opening of the tap, we went with the donors to see where women were collecting water [before],” Yaari told the SA Jewish Report.
She described how women had been going up and down a steep hill for decades. They made the journey two to three times a day, sometimes walking for as long as an hour each way. The water was visibly dirty, she said, raising concerns about the risks associated with drinking and using it.
Community members expressed relief at no longer having to depend on that source of water. Yaari said women spoke about the prospect of protecting their families from waterborne illness and having access to water for personal hygiene.
They also spoke about what the new supply could mean for their economic prospects. “They want to open businesses now that they will have more time and they can use the water to open new businesses,” she said.
Access to water can affect far more than a household’s ability to drink, cook, and wash. When families no longer need to spend hours collecting water, they can redirect that time towards education, paid work, and other activities. For women and girls, who often carry much of the responsibility for collecting water in rural communities, a nearby supply can also reduce the daily burden of these journeys.
Innovation: Africa works to address these challenges by using solar energy to pump water in communities where reliable infrastructure is lacking.
Founded 18 years ago, the organisation operates in South Africa, Uganda, Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, and Cameroon.
In South Africa, its projects have reached villages in several provinces, including Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, and the Eastern Cape. The Okledeni installation uses solar panels to supply the energy needed to pump water, reducing reliance on conventional electricity infrastructure.
However, installing the equipment is only one part of the process. Keeping it operational requires local knowledge, technical skills, and a system for funding maintenance and repairs.
At Okledeni, 14 people from the village worked alongside the contractor for four months, learning to operate, repair, and maintain the solar-powered system. They received certificates of completion at the opening ceremony. Yaari said the training could improve their prospects of finding employment by giving them practical technical skills.
The project also includes a structure intended to support the system over the longer term. A water committee elected by the community signed a memorandum of understanding confirming its ownership of the installation.
The committee has opened a bank account, with each household contributing towards protecting and maintaining the system. This arrangement is intended to help the community take responsibility for the infrastructure and ensure funds are available when maintenance is needed.
For Innovation: Africa, community participation is central to making projects sustainable. A system must continue working after the installation team leaves, or the benefits of the initial investment can be lost.
The Victor Daitz Foundation funded the Okledeni installation. The foundation supports projects exclusively in KwaZulu-Natal and has funded four villages in the province. The donor involved has supported four villages across Africa, including projects in KwaZulu-Natal.
Yaari described how the community responded to the fact that the technology came from Israel. “We mentioned that we’re from Jerusalem,” she said. “It was well received.”
The participants even danced together to the song Jerusalema. For Yaari, the reception was significant because the project brought together Israeli technology and a rural South African community around a practical need.
Innovation: Africa’s work in South Africa has expanded considerably since the organisation first began operating in the country. In a previous interview with the SA Jewish Report, Yaari described how she had initially doubted that South Africa needed its assistance because she believed the country was comparatively wealthy.
Her perspective changed after visiting rural villages and seeing women walking long distances to collect dirty water despite the presence of electricity and other modern amenities in some communities.
Yaari said the organisation intends to continue expanding its work in South Africa and elsewhere on the continent.
- Sivan Yaari was hosted on 13 October by the Union of Jewish Women at the Rabbi Cyril Harris Community Centre.

articles.title: Race for critical minerals swallows Congolese mining city - Kuwait Times
articles.summary: Race for critical minerals swallows Congolese mining city  Kuwait Times
articles.full_text:
KOLWEZI: From his yard, Chibang Kasump watches miners come and go day and night as they dig for copper and cobalt deep beneath his small brick home in the southern Democratic Republic of Congo. The 47-year-old has lived for more than a decade in the Musonoi area of Kolwezi, the country’s mining capital, which sits atop deposits at the center of a global race for critical minerals.
“I bought this house because it was quiet, close to the city centre and near the lake,” he told AFP. “I didn’t know there were minerals beneath my feet. Now I live with a well in my yard.”
The DRC produces around 70 percent of the world’s cobalt, which is key to making batteries and defense technology. It also holds some of the world’s richest copper deposits, a metal in growing demand as countries expand power grids to harness renewable energy. Mining companies and foreign investors have stepped up expansion, exploration and acquisitions. China has invested in the DRC for two decades, and the United States signed a strategic partnership deal with Kinshasa in December to secure supplies for its high-tech industry.
Kasump’s plot lies within the concession of the Tondo Mining Company, a Congolese firm whose site borders a vast copper and cobalt deposit run by the Chinese company Commus. Ahead of industrial mining, artisanal miners, known as diggers, have moved in right up to Kasump’s yard. Across Kolwezi, in the heart of Africa’s copper belt, open-pit mines are gradually eating into neighborhoods and concessions overlap. In Musonoi, houses have numbers spray-painted on them. “All the houses are identified for relocation,” said local administrative official Kazadi Roger. “The mining company is going to provide compensation, but people still don’t know when they’ll be leaving.”
Under Congolese mining law, a land title gives no rights to minerals in the subsoil, but occupants must be compensated if their land is expropriated. Kasump initially refused to move but said “with the pollution, the explosions linked to the extraction, I ended up saying ‘yes’”. He still does not know how much he will receive or where he will go. Dumper trucks rumble nonstop along a road cut by the neighboring Chinese mine, dust settles on rooftops and rainwater seeps into houses cracked by the mining.
Under a white tarpaulin beside his house, a shaft drops about 100 meters (328 feet), where some 30 men hack at the rock with pickaxes while a pump sends air down to them. A human chain hauls the ore, mostly copper, to the surface by rope. Timber props line the walls, but even a small collapse can be fatal. Some diggers earn around $500 a month, others much less, depending on how much ore they recover and its quality.
Diggers say the artisanal mining zones (ZEA) provided for by law are too few. “Everywhere, concessions have already been granted,” said Sylvestre Petit-Petit, the artisanal miners’ local representative. As a result, many work in private concessions, often without authorization, and some break into industrial mines. “Over there, they’re shooting at us,” one miner said, adding he had lost “several friends” that way. The ore is washed, sold to traders who are often Chinese, and partly processed before export.
“The mines advance; the city retreats,” said Aaron Niumbi, a young resident of another Kolwezi neighborhood who also faces having to move because of Commus’s expansion plans. — AFP

articles.title: ECOWAS, OECD target investment, trade growth to accelerate West African integration - The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.summary: ECOWAS, OECD target investment, trade growth to accelerate West African integration  The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.full_text:
The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) are strengthening cooperation to attract investment, expand regional trade and accelerate economic integration across West Africa, with priorities spanning infrastructure, agriculture, capital markets and critical minerals.
The renewed commitment followed talks between the President of the ECOWAS Commission, General Birame Diop, and OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann at the organisation’s headquarters in Paris, France, on October 1, 2026.
The discussions focused on translating the ECOWAS-OECD Memorandum of Understanding, signed in October 2025, into practical initiatives capable of supporting regional development and improving economic opportunities across West Africa.
Diop reaffirmed ECOWAS’s commitment to the partnership, stressing that delivering results would require sustained political commitment, technical cooperation and adequate resources from both institutions.
He also briefed Cormann on the outcomes of the 69th Ordinary Summit of the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government, including the adoption of the Compact for the Future of Regional Integration and ongoing institutional reforms.
The ECOWAS Commission president said the new leadership was determined to strengthen implementation of agreed policies and programmes, highlighting the need for effective institutions and improved regulatory frameworks to attract investment and support regional economic transformation.
Cormann reaffirmed the OECD’s commitment to deepening cooperation with ECOWAS under the Enhanced OECD-Africa Partnership, highlighting the economic potential of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and the importance of open markets in promoting sustainable growth.
He also invited ECOWAS to participate in the OECD Africa Partnership Board, which provides a platform for contributing to the strategic direction of the partnership.
The two institutions identified investment promotion, foreign direct investment, capital market development, food security, agricultural transformation and infrastructure connectivity as priority areas for cooperation.
They also highlighted opportunities to develop critical minerals value chains, strengthen governance and institutional capacity, and improve the competitiveness of West African economies.
For the region, the priorities are significant as ECOWAS seeks to improve economic cooperation among member states and translate regional agreements into practical development outcomes.
The discussions also addressed the need to integrate peace and security considerations into development programmes, strengthen capital markets and explore analytical support for the proposed ECOWAS single currency programme.
During a high-level dialogue involving regional and international institutions, OECD member countries and West African partners, Diop emphasised that strong institutions, effective competition policies and a favourable business environment were essential to attracting investment.
The OECD expressed readiness to support ECOWAS through policy advice, peer learning, governance assessments and capacity development, particularly in implementing the AfCFTA, improving infrastructure connectivity and promoting investment.
Both institutions plan to strengthen technical consultations, establish a joint coordination mechanism, designate institutional focal points and develop a joint work programme aligned with their memorandum of understanding.
The proposed measures are intended to move the partnership beyond policy dialogue towards practical cooperation that supports trade, investment and sustainable economic development across West Africa.
In another development, ECOWAS urged member states to strengthen their statistical systems and protect the independence of national statistics agencies, warning through its latest regional training initiative of the need for more reliable data to guide policymaking and development planning.
The call followed a five-day workshop for statistical managers from ECOWAS member states and Mauritania, held in Monrovia, Liberia. The training focused on improving the management and coordination of national statistical institutions responsible for producing data used in government planning and policy decisions.
The workshop was organised under the World Bank-funded Project for the Harmonising and Improving of Statistics in West and Central Africa (HISWACA).
ECOWAS Commission Director of Research and Statistics, Samson Bel-Aube Nougbodohoue, urged member-states in participation to apply the knowledge gained in their institutions and share it with their teams. He also acknowledged the support of the Liberian government and the Liberia Institute of Statistics and Geo-information Services.
Member-states in participation called for stronger leadership of national statistical systems, better coordination among institutions that produce data and faster implementation of national quality-assurance frameworks.
They also stressed the need to safeguard the professional independence of statistics agencies, an important consideration for ensuring that official figures remain credible and free from political interference.
The recommendations also addressed the growing role of artificial intelligence in official statistics. Participants advocated its responsible use, alongside the diversification of data sources and improved communication to make statistical information more accessible and useful to policymakers and the public.
They urged ECOWAS to support training in generative artificial intelligence, promote the exchange of expertise among member states and provide technical assistance and peer reviews to improve national statistical standards. Translating international statistical guidelines into Community languages was also identified as a way to make them more accessible across the region.

articles.title: IMF Raises Nigeria’s 2026 Growth Forecast to 4.2% on Improved Economic Stability - Investors King
articles.summary: IMF Raises Nigeria’s 2026 Growth Forecast to 4.2% on Improved Economic Stability  Investors King
articles.full_text:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has upgraded Nigeria’s 2026 economic growth forecast to 4.2% from 4.1%, citing improving economic stability and a more favourable outlook for the country.
The revised projection, contained in the IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook, represents an increase of 0.1 percentage point from the Fund’s earlier estimate of 4.1%.
The international financial institution also expects Nigeria’s economy to expand by 4.3% in 2027, suggesting continued economic growth despite uncertainties affecting international financial and commodity markets.
The upward revision comes as Nigeria continues to implement monetary, fiscal and foreign exchange reforms intended to strengthen economic stability, improve market confidence and create conditions for sustainable investment.
For businesses and investors, the improved outlook is significant because macroeconomic stability plays an important role in financial planning, capital allocation and long-term investment decisions.
Greater predictability in exchange rate conditions, inflation expectations and government economic policies can help businesses assess operating costs and future returns more effectively.
The IMF’s assessment indicates that Nigeria’s economic prospects are also benefiting from favourable terms of trade, which can strengthen the country’s external position when export earnings improve relative to import costs.
As a major crude oil producer, Nigeria can benefit from elevated international petroleum prices through stronger export receipts and potentially higher government revenue.
However, the extent of those gains depends on domestic oil production, export volumes and the proportion of earnings available after operational and contractual obligations.
Higher global energy prices can also increase domestic fuel and transportation costs, creating additional pressures for manufacturers, service providers and households.
The IMF’s revised forecast therefore reflects an improving economic outlook rather than an expectation that all sectors will experience the same level of growth.
Nigeria’s recent reforms have focused on strengthening foreign exchange market operations, improving monetary policy effectiveness and rebuilding external financial buffers.
These developments are important for foreign investors assessing the risks associated with Nigerian assets and businesses seeking access to international financing.
For domestic companies, a more stable economic environment could support investment decisions that were previously constrained by exchange rate uncertainty and unpredictable input costs.
Nevertheless, sustained economic expansion will require improvements beyond monetary and foreign exchange management.
Nigeria continues to face structural challenges involving electricity supply, transportation infrastructure, insecurity, agricultural productivity and access to affordable business financing.
Addressing these constraints will be important in determining whether the economy can maintain growth above 4% over the medium term.
The IMF has previously emphasised the need for policies that support private-sector investment, improve productivity and strengthen Nigeria’s capacity to withstand external economic shocks.
It has also encouraged continued fiscal discipline and the protection of priority spending, particularly in areas capable of supporting long-term economic development.
The Fund’s latest outlook comes against a difficult global economic environment marked by geopolitical tensions, elevated energy prices and concerns about government debt.
In its October assessment, the IMF projected global economic growth of 3.1% in 2026, placing Nigeria’s anticipated expansion above the worldwide average.
However, the figures are not directly equivalent measures of economic prosperity, as differences in population growth, productivity and economic structure influence how overall GDP expansion affects individual countries.
For Nigeria, stronger economic performance could improve the outlook for corporate earnings, investment activity and government revenue if the projected expansion is sustained.
The country’s ability to attract productive investment will remain particularly important as policymakers seek to deepen industrial activity and diversify economic growth.
The IMF’s latest revision provides a positive signal about Nigeria’s economic direction, but the strength of future performance will depend on continued policy consistency, improved infrastructure and greater private-sector participation.
With growth now projected at 4.2% in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027, attention will increasingly turn to whether Nigeria can convert improved macroeconomic conditions into sustained investment, higher productivity and broader economic opportunities.

articles.title: Planning Minister outlines 67% private sector investment target and African integration vision at World Bank-IMF meetings - Daily News Egypt
articles.summary: Planning Minister outlines 67% private sector investment target and African integration vision at World Bank-IMF meetings  Daily News Egypt
articles.full_text:
Egypt aims to increase the private sector’s share of total national investments to 67% by 2030, up from 57.7% in the 2025/2026 fiscal year and 43.1% in 2023/2024, Minister of Planning and Economic Development Ahmed Rostom announced.
Speaking at a panel discussion titled “Africa’s Promising Future: Structural Reforms, Trade Integration, and Private Sector-Led Growth” during the 81st Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok, Rostom said the government plans to achieve this target by implementing its State Ownership Policy, ensuring competitive neutrality, streamlining administrative procedures, and expanding single-window services for investors.
Rostom stated that the Egyptian economy registered a real GDP growth rate of 5.1% in the 2025/2026 fiscal year. He added that total foreign exchange assets reached $73.1bn, while the overall balance of payments recorded a surplus of $6.4bn over the same period.
In the energy sector, the minister noted that the full settlement of arrears owed to international oil companies in June 2026 helped restore confidence in Egypt’s energy market. He said Egypt is expanding renewable energy projects in partnership with the private sector, targeting a 42% share of clean energy in its energy mix by 2030.
Addressing broader regional issues, Rostom argued that Africa has historically been treated primarily as a source of raw agricultural goods and minerals without sufficient local industrial processing. He stressed the importance of industrial deepening across the continent to capture higher value-add, strengthen supply chains, and generate local energy and employment.
“For decades, Africa remained treated as a food basket, without achieving sufficient industrial deepening,” Rostom said. “The real challenge for Africa lies in the speed of converting structural reforms into sustainable job opportunities for youth.”
Rostom also highlighted the Infrastructure Financing Guarantee Mechanism as a practical framework for regional cooperation to attract investment into major development projects. He cited the full implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), the simplification of customs procedures, cross-border electrical interconnections, and green hydrogen initiatives as critical elements for regional value chain integration and energy security.

articles.title: Egypt discusses economic reforms at IMF-World Bank meetings in Thailand - Economy - Business - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Egypt discusses economic reforms at IMF-World Bank meetings in Thailand - Economy - Business  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
Egyptian ministers have discussed economic reforms, trade and investment opportunities, and development financing with World Bank officials and regional counterparts on the sidelines of the 2026 annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group in Bangkok, Thailand.
The meetings, which began on Monday and run through 18 October, come as Egypt seeks to attract investment, expand private sector participation and advance its national economic reform program amid ongoing global economic uncertainty.
Egypt’s Minister of Planning and Economic Development Ahmed Rostom and Minister of International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty met Ousmane Dione, the World Bank Group’s vice-president for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (MENAAP), and Senior Vice-President for Development Economics Michael Kremer.
The talks focused on bilateral development cooperation, Egypt’s economic performance and development priorities, and the government’s National Economic Transformation Program. Rostom highlighted Egypt’s GDP growth of 5.1 percent in the 2025/2026 fiscal year, which ended in June 2026.
The minister also confirmed that the government is currently finalizing the National Economic Transformation Program, which aims to transform plans for macroeconomic stability into tangible improvements through improved allocation of investments, increased energy production and efficiency, and expanded energy use and exports.
For his part, Dione affirmed the World Bank’s readiness to provide all necessary support and expertise to the Egyptian government for the preparation and implementation of the program.
Egypt is also working on implementing a package of structural measures to enhance competitiveness, improve the business environment, and build a more resilient economy that is capable of withstanding external shocks, according to Rostom.
The discussions come amid continued uncertainty stemming from the Middle East conflict, trade tensions and higher global energy and food prices.
The IMF projects Egypt’s current account deficit to widen from 4.2 percent of GDP in 2025 to 4.9 percent in 2027, while economic growth is forecast to reach 5.1 percent in 2026 before slowing to 4.7 percent in 2027.
Egyptian Finance Minister Ahmed Kouchouk met his Jordanian counterpart, Abdel Hakim Al-Shibli, to discuss cooperation on fiscal policy, debt management and financing challenges, as well as opportunities to expand bilateral trade and investment.
Kouchouk highlighted the potential for greater coordination and the exchange of expertise on fiscal policies and debt management. He also stressed the importance of developing joint investment projects to create opportunities for Egyptian and Jordanian companies and increase private sector participation.
The private sector accounted for 57.7 percent of Egypt’s total investment in the 2025/2026 fiscal year, according to official figures.
Kouchouk also met Christian Yoka, his counterpart from the Republic of the Congo, to discuss strengthening bilateral economic ties, expanding private sector cooperation and diversifying trade within the framework of African integration and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The two sides discussed exchanging expertise in fiscal reform, domestic resource mobilisation, debt management and policies to support private investment. They also explored ways to strengthen cooperation with multilateral development banks to bolster Africa’s position in the global economy.
Separately, Abdelatty expressed Egypt’s interest in expanding cooperation with the Saudi Fund for Development (SFD) in areas of shared priority to support sustainable and inclusive economic growth.
He made the remarks during a meeting with the fund’s CEO, Sultan bin Abdulrahman Al-Marshad.
The SFD is Saudi Arabia’s main development institution for international cooperation. It provides development loans to developing and least developed countries and manages humanitarian grants, technical assistance and disaster relief programs funded by the Saudi government.
The two sides discussed the role of Arab development finance institutions, including the SFD, in providing flexible financing mechanisms to support economic stability, strengthen regional resilience to crises and advance sustainable development.
They also reviewed economic and geopolitical challenges arising from escalating regional tensions and their impact on developing economies, supply chains and financing costs, as well as opportunities to expand trilateral cooperation across Africa.

articles.full_text:
The trade relationship between Ghana and the United Kingdom (UK) has surpassed GBP1.6 billion, with significant opportunities still available to expand bilateral trade and investment, Alastair Long, His Majesty’s Trade Commissioner for Africa, has said.
Speaking in an interview with the media at the UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce’s (UKGCC) UK-Ghana Trade and Investment Summit 2026, themed “A Decade of Trust, A Future Always On: Scaling the UK-Ghana Growth Partnership,” His Majesty’s Trade Commissioner said the existing trade relationship provides a strong foundation for deeper economic cooperation between the two countries.
He noted that the UK is particularly interested in expanding trade across multiple sectors while ensuring that increased commercial activity translates into jobs, investment and sustainable livelihoods in both economies.
Alastair Long highlighted Ghanaian agricultural exports to the UK as an important part of the relationship, pointing to products such as mangoes and bananas that are increasingly available to British consumers.
He said the two countries have the opportunity to build on their existing trade framework by increasing the flow of Ghanaian exports to the UK while also creating greater opportunities for UK businesses to invest and expand in Ghana.
According to him, the future of the partnership will increasingly include technology, services, agriculture, and investment, alongside traditional areas of trade.
Alastair Long stressed that the ultimate value of the relationship should be measured not only by the volume of trade but also by the economic opportunities and jobs created behind the figures.
Transforming Trust into Investment and Shared Prosperity
Delivering a keynote address on behalf of Vice President, Prof. Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang, the Deputy Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Hon. Sampson Ahi, described the UK-Ghana Trade & Investment Summit 2026 as a pivotal moment in the evolution of the UK-Ghana economic relationship and a platform for converting a decade of cooperation into tangible investment outcomes.
He highlighted Ghana's strong economic performance, noting that the country recorded 6 per cent GDP growth in 2025, while the economy expanded by a further 6.4 per cent in the first quarter of 2026. He said the figures demonstrate that Ghana is stable, predictable and ready to attract investment.
“These numbers tell every investor in this room that Ghana is predictable, Ghana is stable, and Ghana is ready,” he stated.
Hon. Ahi further underscored the strength of UK-Ghana commercial relations, revealing that UK foreign direct investment in Ghana has reached GBP1.8 billion, supporting more than 670 projects and creating over 44,000 jobs across Ghana’s economy. He also highlighted the recently signed UK-Ghana Growth Partnership for 2026-2028, describing it as a practical roadmap for unlocking investment opportunities and accelerating industrial growth.
Calling for deeper collaboration in manufacturing, logistics, agro-processing, healthcare and the digital economy, he urged investors to take advantage of Ghana's strategic location, growing workforce and preferential access to African markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
To investors gathered, he urged, “Bring your technology. Bring your patient capital. Bring your demand for quality and sustainability. In return, we offer a stable policy environment, a government that listens, and a people whose ingenuity has never been in short supply.”
Further calls for a Stronger Partnership
For her part, Her Excellency the Ghana High Commissioner to the UK and Republic of Ireland, Sabah Zita Benson, called for a stronger Ghana-UK economic partnership focused on investment, value addition, technology transfer, skills development, and job creation.
Speaking at the Summit, she said the UKGCC’s 10 years of existence should serve as a foundation for a stronger partnership between the two countries’ business communities, translating into tangible economic opportunities for citizens.
“Ghana is increasingly looking towards partnerships that promote investments in industrialisation, value addition, technology transfer, skills development and job creation,” she said.
She highlighted Ghana’s strategic position in West Africa and its role as host of the AfCFTA Secretariat as major opportunities for UK investors seeking access to the wider African market.
Benson also urged stronger business-to-business connections and greater support for SMEs, while encouraging the Ghanaian diaspora in the UK to leverage its expertise, networks and investment capacity to support development back home.
“The next decade of UK-Ghana economic relations should consequently be defined not simply by the volume of trade between our countries, but by the quality and impact of our partnerships, the businesses we build, the jobs we create, the skills we develop, the technologies we transfer, and the prosperity we generate together,” she said.
UKGCC: 10 years of Promoting Trade Between Ghana and the UK
The UKGCC is currently celebrating its 10th year anniversary. For its Executive Director, Adjoba Kyiamah, it has been 10 years of developing and hosting impactful platforms to advance trade between Ghana and the UK. This summit is one of those platforms, now in its second consecutive year.
Kyiamah said the 3-day summit is focused on advancing the UK–Ghana Growth Partnership by translating policy alignment into commercially viable private-sector investments, with tangible impact on Ghana’s economy.
Kyiamah also hoped that indigenous Ghanaian businesses would utilise the UK as a launchpad to expand internationally and even evolve into global companies with the UKGCC’s support.
“The UK-Ghana trade partnership works both ways. We want to see more Ghanaian businesses using the UK to access capital, expertise, markets, and global networks as they scale beyond Ghana. The UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce is best placed to facilitate this,” she said.
The three-day UK-Ghana Trade and Investment Summit 2026 is being supported by leading institutions and businesses, including GCB Bank PLC, PwC Ghana LTD., UK Government-funded Ghana Jobs for Economic Transformation (JET), Fidelity Bank Ghana LTD., Ecobank Ghana PLC, Vivo Energy Ghana LTD., Quao Realty, DMA Invest, Aqua Africa, Guinness Ghana Breweries PLC, UniChem Ghana LTD., Kasapreko PLC, and media partner, The Business Year.

articles.summary: IMF Projects Tanzania’s Real GDP To Grow By 6.0% In 2026  Howl.link
articles.full_text:
Dar es Salaam, October 15, 2026 - The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects Tanzania’s real GDP to grow by 6.0% in 2026, from an estimated 5.9% in 2025, placing it among the fastest-growing economies in East Africa and sub-Saharan Africa as a whole, at a time when regional growth is expected to remain stable but uneven.
In it's latest World Economic Outlook, which assesses global and regional prospects amid higher energy prices, geopolitical tensions, and tighter financing conditions, IMF notes that Tanzania’s performance stands out for its consistency, supported by strong investment, structural reforms, and macroeconomic stability. The country’s economy grew by an estimated 5.9% in 2025, building on earlier momentum and positioning it for a further acceleration in 2026.
Inflation is expected to remain contained, a key factor behind the positive assessment. Consumer price inflation in Tanzania is projected at 4.0% in 2026 and 4.2% in 2027, up from 3.3% in 2025. That rate is the lowest among East African Community members and less than half the sub-Saharan Africa average of 8.6% in 2026. For comparison, inflation in sub-Saharan Africa is projected to ease to 8.6% in 2026 and 2027 from 12.6% in 2025, with consumer prices in 2026 rising 15.6% in Nigeria and 4.4% in South Africa.
Tanzania’s external position is also expected to remain broadly stable. The current account deficit is projected at 2.7% of GDP in 2026 and 2.6% in 2027, compared with 2.6% in 2025. That stability is supported by stronger gold exports, improved foreign exchange reserves, and greater exchange-rate flexibility.
Gold remains Tanzania’s largest export earner, and high global gold prices have provided a buffer against higher oil and fertilizer import costs. Tourism has also been a major contributor, with travel earnings reaching $4.3 billion, while transport receipts rose to $2.7 billion.
Exports overall rose 12.8% to $18.6 billion in the year to March 2026, driven by a 38.5% increase in gold exports to $5.2 billion and a 32% rise in manufactured goods exports to $1.8 billion.
IMF notes that oil-importing economies without major natural resources are more affected by higher energy and food prices, while declining official development assistance is a headwind across the region. However, Tanzania has managed to offset some of those pressures through export diversification and investment in productive sectors.
Within East Africa and Southern Africa, Tanzania’s growth projection compares favourably with its neighbours.
Among Tanzania’s southern neighbours, growth in 2026 is projected at 5.6% for Zambia, 2.6% for Malawi, and 1.0% for Mozambique. 5.2% for the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 5.0% for Zimbabwe, 4.4% for Angola and Botswana, 2.6% for Malawi, 2.0% for Namibia, and 1.0% for Mozambique.
Among the continent’s largest economies, the IMF projects 2026 growth of 4.2% for Nigeria, 1.0% for South Africa, and 9.2% for Ethiopia, one of the fastest rates in Africa.
Middle-income countries in sub-Saharan Africa are projected to grow by 3.3% in 2026, compared with 6.4% for low-income countries and 4.2% for oil exporters. Tanzania’s position as a lower-middle-income country growing at 6.0% therefore places it above both the middle-income and oil-exporter averages, and close to the low-income group average.
The growth outlook is underpinned by large-scale investment in infrastructure, agriculture, mining, and services. Major projects anchoring this trajectory include the Standard Gauge Railway connecting Dar es Salaam to Dodoma and onward to Mwanza, the East African Crude Oil Pipeline terminating at Tanga Port, the $42 billion Likong’o-Mchinga LNG project with a final investment decision targeted for 2026, the 2,115 MW Julius Nyerere Hydropower Plant now fully commissioned, and the new Msalato International Airport in Dodoma.
The Bank of Tanzania, IMF, and World Bank all project growth above 6% for 2026 and 2027, supported by investment in railways, roads, airports, agriculture, mining, and sports facilities tied to AFCON 2027 co-hosting.
IMF has also highlighted Tanzania’s tax reforms, noting that coordinated tax administration reforms, including a risk-based approach, staff training, improved case management, and better data quality, led to about a 20% rise in assessed taxable income.
In its chapter on corporate income taxation, the IMF cited Tanzania, together with Guinea and Mali, among commodity exporters relying on foreign mining companies that have recently strengthened their frameworks against tax avoidance.
Tanzania has consistently been ranked by the IMF as one of the more resilient economies in Sub-Saharan Africa. In earlier assessments, the Fund noted that growth remains strong, inflation has stayed within the Bank of Tanzania’s target range, international reserves coverage is adequate, and public spending on priority sectors has increased, while the country’s external position has improved.
However, the fund has also cautioned that strong economic growth should not be viewed as the final goal.
Tanzania’s rapidly growing population, expected to exceed 130 million by 2050, means the country must generate far more productive jobs while improving healthcare, education, and public services. Without faster structural reforms, sustained economic growth may not translate into higher living standards or meaningful poverty reduction.

articles.title: South Sudan Chamber of Commerce pushes for practical AfCFTA implementation at Nairobi summit - Eye Radio
