articles.full_text:
South Sudan Chamber of Commerce pushes for practical AfCFTA implementation at Nairobi summit
NAIROBI — A representative of the South Sudan Chamber of Commerce, John Agou Wuoi, has urged regional business leaders to translate the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) into tangible commercial transactions for farmers, young entrepreneurs, and manufacturers.
Addressing fellow chamber leaders and international delegates in Nairobi on October 15, Wuoi, who serves as Executive Board Member and Director of ICT, Innovation and Digital Transformation at the chamber, stressed that businesses measure regional integration through practical milestones—such as locating customers, crossing borders predictably, securing payments, and accessing finance.
He emphasized that removing friction points remains essential to unlocking true cross-border commerce.
Held under the theme “Driving Africa’s Next Era of Trade,” the summit kicked off with discussions on expanding intra-African commerce, unlocking investment opportunities, and accelerating the continent’s economic transformation.
To bridge policy and execution, Wuoi, representing the South Sudan Chamber of Commerce, outlined a comprehensive four-point agenda at the Africa Commerce and Industry Summit 2026:
- Establishing Local Trade Help Desks: Wuoi emphasized bringing AfCFTA closer to enterprises by guiding small businesses through market requirements, rules of origin, customs documentation, and product standards, ensuring that legal progress matches enterprise readiness in South Sudan.
- Driving Direct Business-Matching: He called for chambers across South Sudan, Kenya, and Uganda to connect enterprises around specific supply and demand gaps in food processing, livestock, logistics, and digital services, supported by rigorous follow-up mechanisms to secure actual purchase orders.
- Investing in Regional Value Chains: Wuoi invited strategic partnerships to tackle infrastructure deficits—such as storage facilities, cold chains, reliable power, and transport—particularly within agricultural processing and renewable energy, ensuring smaller enterprises, women, and youth are integrated into wider trading networks.
- Actionable Advocacy on Trade Barriers: Highlighting the cost of border delays and unexpected charges, he urged chambers to compile empirical evidence of trade bottlenecks and collaborate with governments to track resolutions.
Concluding his address, Wuoi proposed that participating chambers adopt a focused 90-day action plan featuring nominated trade focal points, joint business-matching initiatives, and structured follow-ups on non-tariff barriers to ensure the summit’s commitments deliver measurable economic growth.
The high-level roundtable, moderated by Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI) President Dr. Erick Ruto, took place at the Uhuru Gardens National Monument and Museum in Nairobi.
The session formed part of the landmark three-day continental gathering bringing together more than 5,000 delegates, 350 exhibitors, and over 100 investors from 50 countries to mark KNCCI’s 60th anniversary.
Alongside Wuoi, the executive roundtable featured prominent regional and international trade figures, including Adv. Mtho Xulu, President of the South African Chamber of Commerce and Industry; Mr. Vincent Minja, President of the Tanzania Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture; Mr. Ali Suleiman Amour, Chairman of the Zanzibar National Chamber of Commerce; H.E. Mr. Samad Hassan Zadeh, President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture; Mr. Seyed Mehdi, President of the Kerman Chamber of Commerce; and Mr. Christopher Mugaga, CEO of the Zimbabwe National Chamber of Commerce.

articles.title: A global debt crisis is looming. - vijesti.me
articles.summary: A global debt crisis is looming.  vijesti.me
articles.full_text:
GLOBAL ECONOMY
A global debt crisis is looming.
The global economy is increasingly vulnerable, as ongoing conflicts raise energy prices, fuel inflation and expose weaknesses in the existing debt management system.
The world is approaching a global debt crisis. The war in Iran may have been the spark that ignited the fire, but the dry branches have been piling up for a long time. A decade of debt accumulation, higher interest rates, and increasing refinancing needs have made the world economy increasingly vulnerable to shocks. At the same time, ongoing conflicts are pushing up energy prices, and new inflationary pressures are testing the limits of the existing debt management system.
The outlook is particularly worrying for developing countries, whose public debt is expected to reach $35 trillion by 2025, an increase of 10,5% in just one year. According to the UN Development Programme, “the average developing country now spends about 9,5% of its government revenue on interest payments, the highest share in 25 years.” Thirty-two low-income countries are already in debt distress or at high risk of one. However, debt restructuring negotiations with private creditors take an average of two and a half years, twice as long as before the pandemic.
The fundamental problem is not how much countries owe, but rather the cost and unavailability of new financing. Effective interest costs are rising faster than many countries can bear, given their ability to service their debt with export earnings and budget revenues. This gap could widen further. Even countries where the public debt-to-GDP ratio has stabilized could face serious liquidity problems if they are forced to refinance large amounts of debt at significantly higher interest rates.
This problem is not limited to developing countries. The total interest costs on OECD countries’ debt have exceeded $2 trillion. The US is absorbing huge amounts of capital due to its ever-increasing government borrowing, while the companies that operate the largest AI infrastructure systems themselves are increasingly turning to the bond market. Meanwhile, higher defense spending and new, large budget commitments threaten to push interest rates even higher.
When the world's largest debtor can borrow almost unlimitedly, the price can be paid by countries whose financing needs are incomparably smaller.
This global debt system is unfair and unsustainable. Even countries that have been borrowing cautiously may find themselves under pressure from decisions made elsewhere. Developing economies face an impossible choice: either pay more to refinance existing debt or reduce spending on health, education, infrastructure, and productive investment. The solution cannot lie solely in austerity measures. Debt sustainability ultimately depends on the productive capacity from which future economic growth, income, and foreign exchange reserves will flow. Fiscal discipline is important, but it is equally important to protect the public investment necessary to keep debt sustainable.
The good news is that the international community does not have to start from scratch. Several reforms agreed last year in Seville, at the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, have already shown that the proposed solutions can work in practice. Clauses allowing for the temporary suspension of debt payments are becoming standard; innovative debt-for-development investment arrangements have been trialled; the IMF and the World Bank have just adopted changes to their frameworks for assessing debt sustainability; collective action clauses are becoming more widespread, and a new platform of debtor countries is giving them a stronger voice.
Financial markets are starting to react to these changes. Moody's now considers the possibility of a temporary suspension of debt payments to be a positive credit rating, meaning that the activation of a contractual suspension clause will not be treated as a default. This single change removes one of the main reasons why policymakers have been hesitant to use these clauses.
However, our expert group has identified a serious shortcoming in the implementation of the reforms agreed in Seville: the necessary instruments are in place, but they have not yet become common practice. This is described in detail in the report on the implementation of reforms, which the Debt Expert Group published in October 2026. In the current macroeconomic circumstances, this could become a serious problem. In an emergency, countries cannot wait years for new provisions to be incorporated into contracts or laws. They urgently need a mechanism for temporary debt suspension, modeled on the G20 Debt Service Suspension Initiative launched during the pandemic.
This should be made available to all countries facing acute financial pressures, with multilateral development banks encouraged to engage in such arrangements. By providing immediate liquidity, we can prevent today’s refinancing problems from turning into tomorrow’s solvency crises. At the same time, the volume of concessional financing must be significantly increased and its provision made more predictable. Given that additional sources of lending and refinancing are crucial for debt sustainability, multilateral development banks should increase their resources for concessional lending, expand their guarantee programmes and offer more countercyclical financing. The broader network of public development banks, now linked through the Finance in Common initiative, should also be included in the response to the crisis.
Wherever and whenever feasible, countries should also diversify the currencies in which they borrow, improve domestic debt management and strengthen liquidity buffers, and develop financing strategies that take greater account of currency and refinancing risks.
Finally, debt sustainability analyses need to clearly distinguish liquidity problems from insolvency, taking into account a prolonged period of high interest rates, volatile export earnings, fiscal constraints, and the value of investments that strengthen the economy’s resilience and productive capacity. The recently adopted revision of the IMF-World Bank Debt Sustainability Framework (LIC-DSF) is a step in the right direction. It will encourage both institutions to base their assessments on a longer time horizon, include domestic debt in the analysis, and introduce liquidity indicators—gross financing needs and interest expenses relative to income—to disentangle signals of liquidity problems from indicators of insolvency.
However, these changes will only apply from mid-2027 and will not cover countries that are normally able to borrow on international capital markets. This means that the institutions responsible for implementing key reforms need to decide how to proceed. The G20, particularly during the UK presidency next year, can translate its stated commitment to improving coordination on low- and middle-income country debt into concrete reforms of the Common Debt Restructuring Framework. The IMF and the World Bank can accelerate the implementation of the revised LIC-DSF framework and extend it to countries with access to capital markets. Creditors and debtors can transform debt swaps for development goals from one-off innovative solutions to instruments that can be applied regularly. And debtor countries can build the Debt Platform into a permanent institution.
The debt management architecture agreed in Seville was designed in response to global shocks. The shocks have already arrived, but the implementation of the agreed measures has not yet. Countries that already bear the brunt of the financing burden cannot afford to wait for reforms to catch up with reality.
P. Gentiloni co-chairs the UN Secretary-General's Debt Expert Group and is a former European Commissioner for the Economy;
T. Manuel is the Co-Chair of the UN Secretary-General's Debt Expert Group and former Minister of Finance of the Republic of South Africa;
M. Mohieldin is the UN Special Envoy on Financing for Sustainable Development and Co-Chair of the UN Secretary-General's Debt Expert Group; he was Minister of Investment of Egypt (2004–2010), Senior Vice President of the World Bank Group, and Managing Director of the IMF
The text is signed by Rémy Rioux, Director General of the French Development Agency (AFD), and Yan Wang, Senior Academic Researcher at the Center for Global Development Policy at Boston University.

articles.title: Egypt sees Thailand as gateway to trade and ASEAN cooperation - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Egypt sees Thailand as gateway to trade and ASEAN cooperation  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Egypt’s foreign policy is steadily broadening its horizons, with Asia emerging as an increasingly important pillar of our diplomatic and economic engagement. We are placing longstanding partnerships on a new trajectory; harnessing our solid political ties to forge new opportunities in trade, investment, technology and development across a region of growing global influence.
There has been significant momentum in Egypt’s outreach to Asia, underscored most recently by President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi’s Asian tour of South Korea, Malaysia and Indonesia, which reaffirmed Egypt’s commitment to strengthening its partnerships across the continent and expanding cooperation in political, economic and cultural fields.
Having recently returned from the Philippines, where I participated in the 59th ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, my visit to Thailand offers a further opportunity to advance this engagement and to deepen Egypt’s ties with Southeast Asia.
ASEAN’s economic weight, technological capabilities and growing political influence make it an increasingly important partner for Egypt. Since Egypt’s accession to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia in 2016, we have steadily expanded our engagement with ASEAN members across trade, investment, education and development. We now look forward to taking this relationship further by advancing Egypt’s aspiration to become a Sectoral Dialogue Partner of ASEAN. This reflects our recognition of ASEAN’s growing role in advancing regional stability and economic development, as well as the considerable potential for broader bilateral and multilateral cooperation.
Thailand has been an integral partner in this endeavour and an important bridge to our engagement with ASEAN and the wider Southeast Asian region. Our partnership with Thailand is underpinned by a deep-rooted historical tie. In September 1954, Egypt became the first Arab and African country to establish diplomatic relations with Thailand, laying the foundation for more than seven decades of bilateral relations.
My visit to Bangkok, the first by an Egyptian Foreign Minister since 1996, comes at an important juncture in our bilateral relations. It has provided an opportunity to reinvigorate our institutional mechanisms and translate political dialogue into tangible outcomes.
On this visit we convened the third session of the Joint Ministerial Commission and the Joint Business Forum, building on the eighth round of political consultations held in Cairo in June. These mechanisms are essential to sustaining high-level political dialogue while driving practical cooperation in trade, investment and development.
Marking another step forward, we signed a Memorandum of Understanding between the Thailand International Cooperation Agency and the Egyptian Agency for Partnership for Development. The agreement establishes a framework for joint development initiatives in third countries, particularly in areas of shared interest, aiming to combine our efforts to contribute to poverty alleviation and achieve sustainable development. It also reflects the potential for Egypt and Thailand to leverage their respective expertise and capabilities in support of development across the Global South.
My visit also takes place in my capacity as Egypt’s Governor at the World Bank, as I participate in the Fall Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The convergence of these diplomatic and economic engagements is reflective of a broader reality where development and economic cooperation are no longer peripheral to foreign policy; they are central to it.
This is particularly evident amid persistent geopolitical tensions, mounting debt burdens and widening development financing gaps. For developing countries, reforming the international financial architecture is imperative to address pressing development needs. The same applies to climate action. Countries that have contributed least to climate change are often among those bearing its most severe consequences. We therefore need a global financial system that expands access to concessional development finance, strengthens resilience and enables developing economies to pursue sustainable growth without assuming disproportionate burdens.
Against this backdrop, economic cooperation with Thailand is a particular priority. The potential to expand bilateral trade and investment remains substantial. Thailand brings considerable strengths in manufacturing, agriculture, food production, healthcare and tourism, while Egypt offers a large and growing market, a skilled workforce, modern infrastructure and strategic access to Africa, the Middle East and Europe. Our objective is to encourage more Thai companies to view Egypt not simply as an investment destination, but as a gateway for production and regional distribution, while creating greater opportunities for Egyptian businesses to access Thailand and the wider ASEAN market.
Thai investment in Egypt is already demonstrating the potential of this partnership. Hi-Tech Apparel’s US$20 million sportswear factory in Qantara West, the first Thai industrial investment in Egypt and in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, provides a tangible example of what our economic relationship can deliver.
The regional environment further underscores the importance of resilient economic partnerships. Recent crises and disruptions to navigation in the Red Sea have affected shipping costs, delivery times and global supply chains, reinforcing the shared interest of Egypt and Thailand in secure maritime routes and resilient trade networks.
Egypt continues to invest in strengthening the infrastructure and operational capabilities of the Suez Canal while pursuing measures to enhance the resilience and competitiveness of its economy. The Government Offerings IPO Programme, the State Ownership Policy and the incentives extended to foreign investors form part of a broader effort to strengthen the private sector and create a more conducive investment environment.
Egypt’s engagement with Asia is ultimately part of a broader foreign policy anchored in strategic balance, diversification and mutually beneficial partnerships. We seek constructive relations across regions, grounded in mutual respect and shared interests, while strengthening cooperation with partners that can contribute to a more stable, prosperous and interconnected international order. Within this vision, Southeast Asia and particularly Thailand occupies an increasingly important place in Egypt’s ambitious foreign policy.
